<!-- Definition and symptoms -->
'''Obstructive sleep apnea''' ('''OSA''') is recurrent episodes of [[airway obstruction|narrowing or blockage]] of the [[respiratory tract#Upper respiratory tract|throat]] during [[sleep]].<ref name=NHS2023>{{cite web |title=Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) |url=https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/lungs-and-airways/obstructive-sleep-apnoea |website=www.nhsinform.scot |access-date=27 June 2023 |language=en |archive-date=10 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230510204539/https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/lungs-and-airways/obstructive-sleep-apnoea |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230510204539/https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/lungs-and-airways/obstructive-sleep-apnoea |date=10 May 2023 }}</ref> Symptoms may include [[daytime sleepiness]], [[snoring]], short periods of interrupted breathing, [[nighttime urination]], and headaches in the morning.<ref name=NHS2023/><ref name=Vea2019/> Complications may include [[heart disease]], [[stroke]], [[diabetes]], and [[motor vehicle collisions]].<ref name=Vea2019/>

<!-- Cause and diagnosis -->
Risk factors include being [[overweight]], taking [[sedatives]], large [[tonsils]], smoking, [[nasal congestion]], and family history.<ref name=NHS2023/> The underlying mechanism involves a fall in [[oxygen levels]] which results in partial or complete [[waking]].<ref name=NHS2023/> Symptoms are often first noticed by family or friends rather than the person themselves.<ref name=NHS2023/> Diagnosis is based on an [[apnea–hypopnea index]] (AHI) of at least 5 per hour as measured by [[polysomnography]] or home sleep testing.<ref name=Vea2019/><ref name=NHS2023Diag>{{cite web |title=Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) |url=https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/lungs-and-airways/obstructive-sleep-apnoea#about-obstructive-sleep-apnoea |website=www.nhsinform.scot |access-date=27 June 2023 |language=en |archive-date=10 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230510204539/https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/lungs-and-airways/obstructive-sleep-apnoea#about-obstructive-sleep-apnoea |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230510204539/https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/lungs-and-airways/obstructive-sleep-apnoea#about-obstructive-sleep-apnoea |date=10 May 2023 }}</ref> It is a type of [[sleep apnea]], along with the less common [[central sleep apnea]].<ref name=NHS2023/>

<!-- Treatment and prognosis -->
[[Continuous positive airway pressure]] (CPAP) is the recommended treatment in those with moderate to severe disease.<ref name=Vea2019/> While it improves daytime sleepiness and [[quality of life]], affects on risk of heart disease or death is unclear.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ton |first1=Joey |title=#218 CPAP—Breath of life, or just hot air? |url=https://cfpclearn.ca/tfp218/ |website=CFPCLearn |access-date=16 June 2023 |date=20 August 2018 |archive-date=25 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230325132330/https://cfpclearn.ca/tfp218/ |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230325132330/https://cfpclearn.ca/tfp218/ |date=25 March 2023 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Laratta |first1=Cheryl R. |last2=Ayas |first2=Najib T. |last3=Povitz |first3=Marcus |last4=Pendharkar |first4=Sachin R. |title=Diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults |journal=Canadian Medical Association Journal |date=4 December 2017 |volume=189 |issue=48 |pages=E1481–E1488 |doi=10.1503/cmaj.170296}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gottlieb |first1=Daniel J. |last2=Punjabi |first2=Naresh M. |title=Diagnosis and Management of Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Review |journal=JAMA |date=14 April 2020 |volume=323 |issue=14 |pages=1389 |doi=10.1001/jama.2020.3514}}</ref> [[Weight loss]] and avoiding sedatives are also recommended.<ref name=Vea2019/> Other options may be used in those who cannot tolerate CPAP, including a [[mandibular advancement device]] or surgery.<ref name=NHS2023/><ref name=Vea2019/> [[Life expectancy]] is lower among those effected, particularly if they do not tolerate CPAP.<ref name=Stat2023/>

<!-- Epidemiology and history -->
Obstructive sleep apnea is common; affecting about a billion people worldwide.<ref name=Stat2023>{{cite journal |last1=Slowik |first1=JM |last2=Sankari |first2=A |last3=Collen |first3=JF |title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea. |journal=StatPearls |date=January 2023 |pmid=29083619}}</ref> In the United States it occurs in about 34% of middle aged males and 17% of females.<ref name=Vea2019>{{cite journal |last1=Veasey |first1=Sigrid C. |last2=Rosen |first2=Ilene M. |title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |date=11 April 2019 |volume=380 |issue=15 |pages=1442–1449 |doi=10.1056/NEJMcp1816152}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yeghiazarians |first1=Yerem |last2=Jneid |first2=Hani |last3=Tietjens |first3=Jeremy R. |last4=Redline |first4=Susan |last5=Brown |first5=Devin L. |last6=El-Sherif |first6=Nabil |last7=Mehra |first7=Reena |last8=Bozkurt |first8=Biykem |last9=Ndumele |first9=Chiadi Ericson |last10=Somers |first10=Virend K. |title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Cardiovascular Disease: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association |journal=Circulation |date=20 July 2021 |volume=144 |issue=3 |doi=10.1161/CIR.0000000000000988}}</ref> It occurs more commonly in those over the age of 40.<ref name=NHS2023/> Some countries limit the ability to drive among those affected until the condition is well controlled.<ref name=NHS2023/> Interest in the condition grew in part from [[Charles Dickens]]' novel ''[[The Pickwick Papers|The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club]]'' in 1837; with the link with airway obstruction recognized in the 1960s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guilleminault |first1=Christian |title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea: The Clinical Syndrome and Historical Perspective |journal=Medical Clinics of North America |date=November 1985 |volume=69 |issue=6 |pages=1187–1203 |doi=10.1016/s0025-7125(16)30982-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kryger |first1=Meir H. |last2=Roth |first2=Thomas |last3=Dement |first3=William C. |title=Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine E-Book |date=29 December 2015 |publisher=Elsevier Health Sciences |isbn=978-0-323-37752-2 |page=627 |url=https://www.google.ca/books/edition/Principles_and_Practice_of_Sleep_Medicin/AB-KCwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=&pg=PA627 |language=en |access-date=1 July 2023 |archive-date=1 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230701173648/https://www.google.ca/books/edition/Principles_and_Practice_of_Sleep_Medicin/AB-KCwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=&pg=PA627 |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230701173648/https://www.google.ca/books/edition/Principles_and_Practice_of_Sleep_Medicin/AB-KCwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=&pg=PA627 |date=1 July 2023 }}</ref>
{{TOC limit}}

==Signs and symptoms==
Common symptoms include [[excessive daytime sleepiness]], restless sleep, and loud [[snoring]] (with periods of silence followed by gasps). Less common symptoms are morning [[headaches]]; [[insomnia]]; trouble concentrating; mood changes such as [[irritability]], [[anxiety]], and [[Depression (mood)|depression]]; forgetfulness; increased heart rate or [[blood pressure]]; decreased sex drive; unexplained weight gain; increased urinary frequency or [[nocturia]]; frequent heartburn or [[gastroesophageal reflux disease|gastroesophageal reflux]]; and night sweats.<ref name=cognition>{{cite journal |last1=Caporale |first1=Mina |last2=Palmeri |first2=Rosanna |last3=Corallo |first3=Francesco |last4=Muscarà |first4=Nunzio |last5=Romeo |first5=Laura |last6=Bramanti |first6=Alessia |last7=Marino |first7=Silvia |last8=Lo Buono |first8=Viviana |title=Cognitive impairment in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome: a descriptive review |journal=Sleep and Breathing |date=23 May 2020 |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=29–40 |doi=10.1007/s11325-020-02084-3 |pmid=32447633 |s2cid=218835830 }}</ref>

Many people experience episodes of OSA for only a short period. This can be the result of an upper respiratory infection or [[tonsillitis]].<ref name="pmid22297210">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ezzeddini R, Darabi M, Ghasemi B, Jabbari Moghaddam Y, Abdollahi SH, Temporary spells of OSA syndrome may also occur in individuals who are under the influence of a drug (such as [[Ethanol|alcohol]]).<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.lecturio.com/concepts/obstructive-sleep-apnea/|title= Obstructive Sleep Apnea|website= The Lecturio Medical Concept Library|date= 7 August 2020|access-date= 21 August 2021|archive-date= 21 August 2021|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210821070459/https://www.lecturio.com/concepts/obstructive-sleep-apnea/|url-status= live}} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210821070459/https://www.lecturio.com/concepts/obstructive-sleep-apnea/ |date=21 August 2021 }}</ref>

===Adults===
Typically, an adult or adolescent with severe long-standing OSA will fall asleep for very brief periods in the course of usual daytime activities if given an opportunity to sit or rest. This behavior may be quite dramatic, sometimes occurring during conversations with others at social gatherings.

OSA can cause problems in mentally manipulating non-verbal information, in [[executive functions]] and [[working memory]]. This repeated brain hypoxia is may also cause [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref name="pmid14751008">{{cite journal |last1=Gale |first1=Shawn D. |last2=Hopkins |first2=Ramona O. |title=Effects of hypoxia on the brain: Neuroimaging and neuropsychological findings following carbon monoxide poisoning and obstructive sleep apnea |journal=Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society |date=January 2004 |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=60–71 |doi=10.1017/S1355617704101082 |pmid=14751008 |s2cid=23745738 }}</ref>

===Children===
Excessive sleepiness may occur in children, though it is not typical in young children. Young children instead ordinarily behave as if "over-tired" or "[[hyperactivity|hyperactive]]"; and have behavioral problems like irritability and deficit in attention.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite Gerry |last4=Kirchner |first4=H. Lester |last5=Emancipator |first5=Judith L. |last6=Redline |first6=Susan |date=December 2004 |title=Increased Behavioral Morbidity in School-Aged Children With Sleep-Disordered Breathing |journal=Pediatrics |volume=114 |issue=6 |pages=1640–1648 |doi=10.1542/peds.2004-0103|pmid=15574628 |s2cid=7655711 }}</ref>

Young children are generally thin and may have [[failure to thrive]]. Poor growth occurs for two reasons: the work of breathing is intense enough that calories are burned at high rates even at rest, and the nose and throat are so obstructed that eating is both tasteless and physically uncomfortable. OSA in children, unlike adults, is often caused by obstructive [[tonsil]]s and [[adenoid]]s and may sometimes be cured with [[tonsillectomy]] and [[adenoidectomy]].

This problem can also be caused by excessive weight in children. In this case, the symptoms are more like the symptoms adults feel such as restlessness, exhaustion, etc. If adenotonsillar hypertrophy remains the most common cause of OSA in children,<ref name=Dehlink2016>{{cite journal | vauthors = Dehlink E, Tan HL | title = Update on paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea | journal = Journal of Thoracic Disease | volume = 8 | issue = 2 | pages = 224–235 | date = February 2016 | pmid = 26904263 | pmc = 4739955 | doi = 10.3978/j.issn.2072-1439.2015.12.04 }}</ref><ref name=Jazi2011>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jazi SM, Barati B, Kheradmand A | title = Treatment of adenotonsillar hypertrophy: A prospective randomized trial comparing azithromycin vs. fluticasone | journal = Journal of Research in Medical Sciences | volume = 16 | issue = 12 | pages = 1590–1597 | date = December 2011 | pmid = 22973368 | pmc = 3434901 }}</ref> [[obesity]] can also play a role in the pathophysiology of upper airway obstruction during sleep which can lead to OSA, making obese children more likely to develop the condition.<ref name="Capdevilaetal2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Capdevila OS, Kheirandish-Gozal L, Dayyat E, Gozal D | title = Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea: complications, management, and long-term outcomes | journal = Proceedings of the American Thoracic Society | volume = 5 | issue = 2 | pages = 274–282 | date = February 2008 | pmid = 18250221 | pmc = 2645258 | doi = 10.1513/pats.200708-138MG }}</ref> The recent epidemic increase of obesity prevalence has thus contributed to changes in the prevalence and in the characteristics of pediatric OSA,<ref name="Dayyat2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Dayyat E, Kheirandish-Gozal L, Gozal D | title = Childhood Obstructive Sleep Apnea: One or Two Distinct Disease Entities? | journal = Sleep Medicine Clinics | volume = 2 | issue = 3 | pages = 433–444 | date = September 2007 | pmid = 18769509 | pmc = 2084206 | doi = 10.1016/j.jsmc.2007.05.004 }}</ref> the severity of OSA being proportional to the degree of obesity.<ref name=Kalra2005>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kalra M, Inge T, Garcia V, Daniels S, Lawson L, Curti R, Cohen A, Amin R | display-authors = 6 | title = Obstructive sleep apnea in extremely overweight adolescents undergoing bariatric surgery | journal = Obesity Research | volume = 13 | issue = 7 | pages = 1175–1179 | date = July 2005 | pmid = 16076986 | doi = 10.1038/oby.2005.139 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=Verhulst2009>{{cite journal | vauthors = Verhulst SL, Franckx H, Van Gaal L, De Backer W, Desager K | title = The effect of weight loss on sleep-disordered breathing in obese teenagers | journal = Obesity | volume = 17 | issue = 6 | pages = 1178–1183 | date = June 2009 | pmid = 19265797 | doi = 10.1038/oby.2008.673 | s2cid = 205526401 }}</ref>

Obesity leads to the narrowing of upper airway structure due to fatty infiltration and fat deposits in the anterior [[neck]] region and cervical structures.<ref name=Dehlink2016 /><ref name="Dayyat2008"/> Alongside with the additional weight loading on the [[respiratory system]], it increases the risk of pharyngeal collapsibility while reducing the intrathoracic volume and diaphragm excursion.<ref name="Dayyat2008"/> Moreover, excessive daytime sleepiness resulting from sleep fragmentation can decrease physical activity and thus lead to weight gain (by sedentary habits or increased food intake to overcome [[somnolence]]).<ref name=Bower2000>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bower CM, Gungor A | title = Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea syndrome | journal = Otolaryngologic Clinics of North America | volume = 33 | issue = 1 | pages = 49–75 | date = February 2000 | pmid = 10637344 | doi = 10.1016/s0030-6665(05)70207-3 }}</ref> The obesity-related obstruction of upper airway structure has led some authors to distinguish between two types of OSA in children:<ref name="Capdevilaetal2008"/><ref name="Dayyat2008"/> type I is associated with marked lymphadenoid [[hypertrophy]] without obesity and type II is first associated with obesity and with milder upper airway lymphadenoid [[hyperplasia]]. The two types in children can results in different morbidities and consequences.<ref name="Capdevilaetal2008"/> Weight loss in obese adolescents can reduce [[sleep apnea]].<ref name=Dehlink2016 /><ref name=Verhulst2009 />

==Consequences==
There are physiologic, intermediate and clinical consequences.<ref name = "OSA"/> The physiologic consequences contain hypoxia, sleep fragmentation, autonomic nervous system dysregulation or hyperoxia.<ref name = "OSA"/> The intermediate results regroup inflammation, pulmonary vasoconstriction, general metabolic dysfunction, oxidation of proteins and lipids or increased adiposity.<ref name = "OSA"/> The clinical repercussions are composed by pulmonary hypertension, accidents, obesity, diabetes, different heart diseases or hypertension.<ref name = "OSA">{{cite journal |last1=Foldvary-Schaefer |first1=Nancy R. |last2=Waters |first2=Tina E. |title=Sleep-Disordered Breathing |journal=Continuum: Lifelong Learning in Neurology |date=August 2017 |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=1093–1116 |doi=10.1212/01.CON.0000522245.13784.f6 |pmid=28777178 |s2cid=20852866 }}</ref>

===Children===
Obstructive sleep apnea is the most common Sleep-Disordered Breathing (SDB) and affects up to 11% of children born at term – it is even more common (3 to 6 times more) in children born pre-term.<ref name=Walter2018>{{cite journal | vauthors = Walter LM, Horne RS |s2cid=80862031 |title=Obstructive Sleep-Disordered Breathing in Children; impact on the Developing Brain |journal=Pediatric Respirology and Critical Care Medicine |date=2018 |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=58–64|doi=10.4103/prcm.prcm_16_18 }}</ref> As a SDB, OSA in children can lead to several adverse consequences, also in the long-term with consequences lasting into adulthood.<ref name=Dehlink2016/> The implications of OSA in children are complex and cover a large scope of consequences: when it is left untreated, OSA can lead to morbidity affecting many different domains of life (organs, body systems, behavioral disturbance, [[depression (mood)|depression]], decreased [[quality of life]], etc.).<ref name=Dayyat2008/> Therefore, nocturnal symptoms indicating the presence of OSA (e.g. [[snoring]], gasping, restless sleep and excessive energy used to breathe during sleep) are associated with daytime symptoms such as concentration and learning difficulties and irritability, neurocognitive development impairment, decreased school performance and behavioral difficulties.<ref name=Dehlink2016 /> For example, SDB such as OSA contributes to hyperactive behavior that can lead to the diagnosis and treatment of [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] (ADHD). However, once the SDB is treated, the hyperactive behavior can improve, and the treatment can be stopped.<ref name=Chervin2001>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chervin RD, Archbold KH | title = Hyperactivity and polysomnographic findings in children evaluated for sleep-disordered breathing | journal = Sleep | volume = 24 | issue = 3 | pages = 313–320 | date = May 2001 | pmid = 11322714 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/24.3.313 | doi-access = free }}</ref> [[Obesity]] also has an impact on the consequences of OSA and lead to different manifestations or severity.<ref name=Dayyat2008 /> Studies have shown that, contrary to adults, children with obstructive sleep-disordered breathing are able to maintain cerebral oxygenation. However, the condition still has effects on the brain and can lead to adverse neurocognitive and behavioral sequelae. It is particularly concerning as those consequences happen while the brain is still developing.<ref name=Walter2018 /> The degree to which the sleep is disturbed and fragmented has been significantly linked to the severity of the consequences, the latter having the possibility to decrease once the sleep is improved.<ref name=Capdevilaetal2008/> It is more the disruption of sleep processes than the total amount of sleep the child experience that generates the adverse consequences on the child's daytime functioning;<ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> it contributes to the hyperactivity for example.<ref name=Chervin2001 />

Children with OSA may experience learning and memory deficits and OSA has also been linked to lowered childhood IQ scores.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Halbower|first1=Ann C|last2=Degaonkar|first2=Mahaveer|last3=Barker|first3=Peter B|last4=Earley|first4=Christopher J|last5=Marcus|first5=Carole L|last6=Smith|first6=Philip L|last7=Prahme|first7=M. Cristine|last8=Mahone|first8=E. Mark|date=2006|title=Childhood Obstructive Sleep Apnea Associates with Neuropsychological Deficits and Neuronal Brain Injury|journal=PLOS Medicine|volume=3|issue=8|pages=e301|doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.0030301|pmc=1551912|pmid=16933960}}</ref>

====Neurocognitive and behavioral====
Nocturnal sleep fragmentation has been linked to neurocognitive impairments, therefore, the identification of SDB such as OSA is crucial in children, those impairments having the possibility to be reversible with the appropriate treatment for the sleep disorder.<ref name=O'Brien2004>{{cite journal | vauthors = O'Brien LM, Mervis CB, Holbrook CR, Bruner JL, Smith NH, McNally N, McClimment MC, Gozal D | display-authors = 6 | title = Neurobehavioral correlates of sleep-disordered breathing in children | journal = Journal of Sleep Research | volume = 13 | issue = 2 | pages = 165–172 | date = June 2004 | pmid = 15175097 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2869.2004.00395.x | s2cid = 25860827 }}</ref> The neurocognitive and behavioral dysfunctions commonly present in children with OSA include the following: hyperactivity, [[impulsivity]], aggressive behaviors,<ref name=Dayyat2008 /><ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> low social and communication abilities and reduced adaptive skills.<ref name=Dehlink2016 />
Children with OSA commonly show cognitive deficits, resulting in attention and [[Attentional control|concentration]] difficulties, as well as lower academic performance and [[Intelligence quotient|IQ]].<ref name=Dehlink2016 /><ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> Poor academic performances have been linked to OSA and suggested to result from cortical and sympathetic arousals and [[hypoxemia]] which affects [[memory consolidation]].<ref name=Goyal2018>{{cite journal | vauthors = Goyal A, Pakhare AP, Bhatt GC, Choudhary B, Patil R | title = Association of pediatric obstructive sleep apnea with poor academic performance: A school-based study from India | journal = Lung India | volume = 35 | issue = 2 | pages = 132–136 | date = 2018 | pmid = 29487248 | pmc = 5846262 | doi = 10.4103/lungindia.lungindia_218_17 }}</ref> A study with Indian children affected by OSA has shown poor school grades, including mathematics, science, language and physical education. This study allowed to see the overall impact of OSA on learning abilities associated with language or numeracy skills, and physical development.<ref name=Goyal2018 /> It has been suggested that the deficits in academic performance related to OSA could be mediated through reduced [[executive functions]] or language skills,<ref name=Galland2015>{{cite journal | vauthors = Galland B, Spruyt K, Dawes P, McDowall PS, Elder D, Schaughency E | s2cid = 20590026 | title = Sleep Disordered Breathing and Academic Performance: A Meta-analysis | journal = Pediatrics | volume = 136 | issue = 4 | pages = e934–946 | date = October 2015 | pmid = 26347434 | doi = 10.1542/peds.2015-1677 }}</ref> those domains contributing highly to learning abilities and behavior. The deficits in school performance can nevertheless be improved if [[Tonsillectomy|adenotonsillectomy]] is performed on children to treat the OSA.<ref name=Galland2015 /> It is thus crucial to identify the OSA for children with school difficulties; many cases remaining unnoticed.<ref name=Galland2015 />

As studies have shown that learning skills and behaviors can be improved if the OSA is treated,<ref name=Dehlink2016 /><ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> the neurocognitive and behavioral deficits are thus at least partly reversible.<ref name=Dayyat2008 /> This reversible dimension has been postulated to be negatively correlated to the duration of the symptoms, which would mean that the longer the OSA is left untreated, the less reversible are the consequences.<ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 />

====Physical====
Similarly to adults, OSA in children is linked to a higher risk for [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular morbidities]],<ref name=Dayyat2008 /><ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> due to increased [[Sympathetic nervous system|sympathetic]] activity and impaired cardiac autonomic control.<ref name=Walter2018 /> Amongst the cardiovascular dysfunctions resulting from OSA, we can find systemic [[hypertension]]<ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> and [[blood pressure]] dysregulation<ref name=Dehlink2016 /><ref name=Amin2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Amin R, Somers VK, McConnell K, Willging P, Myer C, Sherman M, McPhail G, Morgenthal A, Fenchel M, Bean J, Kimball T, Daniels S | s2cid = 1736152 | display-authors = 6 | title = Activity-adjusted 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure and cardiac remodeling in children with sleep disordered breathing | journal = Hypertension | volume = 51 | issue = 1 | pages = 84–91 | date = January 2008 | pmid = 18071053 | doi = 10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.107.099762 | doi-access = free }}</ref> (elevated blood pressure, or variability of the blood pressure for example<ref name=Walter2018 />). The variability of the blood pressure has been shown to be correlated with the severity of the symptoms such as the frequency of the [[apnea]] and [[hypopnea]].<ref name=Amin2008 /> [[Pulmonary hypertension]] is also common amongst the cardiovascular problems resulting from OSA.<ref name=Dehlink2016 /> Children with obstructive sleep-disordered breathing also show a faster heart rate during wakefulness and during sleep.<ref name=Amin2008 />

In adult patients, OSA has been shown to be associated with [[insulin resistance]].<ref name=Ip2002>{{cite journal |last1=Ip |first1=Mary S. M. |last2=Lam |first2=Bing |last3=Ng |first3=Matthew M. T. |last4=Lam |first4=Wah Kit |last5=Tsang |first5=Kenneth W. T. |last6=Lam |first6=Karen S. L. |author-link6=Karen Lam (researcher)|title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea Is Independently Associated with Insulin Resistance |journal=American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine |date=1 March 2002 |volume=165 |issue=5 |pages=670–676 |doi=10.1164/ajrccm.165.5.2103001 |pmid=11874812 }}</ref> In children, [[metabolism|metabolic]] consequences of OSA are complicated to assess as they can also be associated to [[puberty]] and [[obesity]] (if present).<ref name=Dehlink2016 /> However, when OSA is associated with obesity, the interaction of the two conditions can lead to metabolic disturbances such as insulin resistance and altered [[Hyperlipidemia|lipidemia]],<ref name=Dayyat2008 /> [[liver disease]], [[abdominal obesity|abdominal adiposity]] and [[metabolic syndrome]]. Obesity interact with those effects.<ref name=Amin2008 />

====Bed wetting====
Children with OSA also show a higher risk for [[nocturnal enuresis]]<ref name=Dehlink2016 /><ref name=Basha2009>{{cite journal |last1=Basha |first1=Suzanne |last2=Bialowas |first2=Christie |last3=Ende |first3=Kevin |last4=Szeremeta |first4=Wasyl |title=Effectiveness of Adenotonsillectomy in the Resolution of Nocturnal Enuresis Secondary to Obstructive Sleep Apnea |journal=The Laryngoscope |date=2005 |volume=115 |issue=6 |pages=1101–1103 |doi=10.1097/01.MLG.0000163762.13870.83 |pmid=15933530 |s2cid=44686421 }}</ref> and it is hypothesized to be caused by an excessive production of [[urine]],<ref name=Goyal2018 /><ref name=Barone2009>{{cite journal | vauthors = Barone JG, Hanson C, DaJusta DG, Gioia K, England SJ, Schneider D | s2cid = 7324455 | title = Nocturnal enuresis and overweight are associated with obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Pediatrics | volume = 124 | issue = 1 | pages = e53–59 | date = July 2009 | pmid = 19564269 | doi = 10.1542/peds.2008-2805 }}</ref> impaired performance of the [[bladder]] and [[urethra]]<ref name="Brooks2003">{{cite journal |last1=Brooks |first1=Lee J. |last2=Topol |first2=Howard I. |title=Enuresis in children with sleep apnea |journal=The Journal of Pediatrics |date=May 2003 |volume=142 |issue=5 |pages=515–518 |doi=10.1067/mpd.2003.158 |pmid=12756383 }}</ref> or an inability to suppress the nocturnal bladder contraction, due to a failure to arouse.<ref name=Barone2009 /><ref name=Brooks2003 /> The risk for nocturnal enuresis increases with the severity of the sleep-disordered breathing: the more respiratory events per hour of sleep, the higher is the risk for nocturnal enuresis.<ref name=Brooks2003 /> Obesity may also play a role as it is associated with OSA and with nocturnal [[diuresis]] (due to unhealthy diet). The interaction between OSA and obesity might thus result in nocturnal enuresis.<ref name=Barone2009 /> Considering the high prevalence of nocturnal enuresis amongst children with sleep-disordered breathing, it is important to consider the latter in the [[differential diagnosis]] of nocturnal enuresis as the treatment of the sleep disorder might have a favourable therapeutic effect on the enuresis.<ref name="Weissbach2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Weissbach A, Leiberman A, Tarasiuk A, Goldbart A, Tal A | title = Adenotonsilectomy improves enuresis in children with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome | journal = International Journal of Pediatric Otorhinolaryngology | volume = 70 | issue = 8 | pages = 1351–1356 | date = August 2006 | pmid = 16504310 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijporl.2006.01.011 }}</ref><ref name=Basha2009 /><ref name=Brooks2003 /> For example, an [[Tonsillectomy|adenotonsillectomy]] performed to reduce OSA has a positive impact on nocturnal enuresis.<ref name=Weissbach2006 /><ref name=Goyal2018 /> A study has shown that this surgery has 60–75% chance to resolve the nocturnal enuresis completely, and 80–85% chance to reduce its symptoms alongside others symptoms of OSA.<ref name=Basha2009 />

====Other====
Contrary to adults, [[excessive daytime sleepiness]] (EDS) is not the most commonly reported symptoms in children with OSA.<ref name=O'Brien2004 /> However, using objective questionnaires, it is possible to notice that the frequency of EDS in children is higher than what is reported by the parents or caretakers (40–50%).<ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> And the risk for EDS is even increased when OSA is associated with [[obesity]].<ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /><ref name=Dayyat2008 />

Due to all the consequences and symptoms it generates, OSA in children lead to a significant decrease in the [[quality of life]],<ref name=Capdevilaetal2008 /> the decrease being even higher when obesity is present.<ref name=Dayyat2008 /> The quality of life can however be improved with the treatment of OSA.<ref name=Dayyat2008 /> SBD have also been linked to a higher rate of [[internalizing disorder]]s such as [[anxiety]] and [[depression (mood)|depression]].<ref name="Carotenuto2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Carotenuto M, Esposito M, Parisi L, Gallai B, Marotta R, Pascotto A, Roccella M | title = Depressive symptoms and childhood sleep apnea syndrome | journal = Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment | volume = 8 | pages = 369–373 | date = 2012 | pmid = 22977304 | pmc = 3430390 | doi = 10.2147/NDT.S35974 }}</ref> Indeed, depressive symptoms have shown to be higher in children with OSA,<ref name=Carotenuto2012 /> especially in males.<ref name="Yilmaz2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Yilmaz E, Sedky K, Bennett DS | title = The relationship between depressive symptoms and obstructive sleep apnea in pediatric populations: a meta-analysis | journal = Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine | volume = 9 | issue = 11 | pages = 1213–1220 | date = November 2013 | pmid = 24235907 | pmc = 3805811 | doi = 10.5664/jcsm.3178 }}</ref> Once again, the severity of depressive symptoms is positively correlated with the severity of the SBD.<ref name=Carotenuto2012 /> It also interacts with obesity as obese children have higher risk to show depressive symptoms and obesity can cause OSA.<ref name=Yilmaz2013 /> The link can also go the other way around with the depression inducing obesity (due to [[overeating]]) which worsens the OSA. [[Tonsillectomy|Adenotonsillectomy]] can decrease the intensity of the depressive symptoms.<ref name=Yilmaz2013 />

Other consequences of a disturbed sleep in children with OSA comprise [[anhedonia]]<ref name="Crabtree2004">{{cite journal | vauthors = Crabtree VM, Varni JW, Gozal D | title = Health-related quality of life and depressive symptoms in children with suspected sleep-disordered breathing | journal = Sleep | volume = 27 | issue = 6 | pages = 1131–1138 | date = September 2004 | pmid = 15532207 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/27.6.1131 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=Carotenuto2012 /> increased [[fatigue]] and decreased interest in daily activities, which in turn can affect the child's social relationships.<ref name=Dayyat2008 />

===Adults===
While there are some similarities between adults and children, OSA does not have the same consequences in both populations.<ref name="Alsubie">{{cite journal | vauthors = Alsubie HS, BaHammam AS | title = Obstructive Sleep Apnoea: Children are not little Adults | journal = Paediatric Respiratory Reviews | volume = 21 | pages = 72–79 | date = January 2017 | pmid = 27262609 | doi = 10.1016/j.prrv.2016.02.003 }}</ref> Examples of similarities are the [[snoring]] – which is the most common complaint in both pediatric OSA and OSA in adults<ref name="Alsubie" /> – variability of [[blood pressure]] and [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular morbidities]].<ref name="Young2004">{{cite journal |last1=Young |first1=Terry |last2=Skatrud |first2=J |last3=Peppard |first3=PE |title=Risk Factors for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults |journal=JAMA |date=28 April 2004 |volume=291 |issue=16 |pages=2013–2016 |doi=10.1001/jama.291.16.2013 |pmid=15113821 |s2cid=12315855 }}</ref> A major difference is the [[excessive daytime sleepiness]] (EDS) which is commonly reported in adult OSA,<ref name="McNicholas2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = McNicholas WT | title = Diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea in adults | journal = Proceedings of the American Thoracic Society | volume = 5 | issue = 2 | pages = 154–160 | date = February 2008 | pmid = 18250207 | doi = 10.1513/pats.200708-118MG }}</ref> while it is not very common in pediatric OSA.<ref name="Alsubie" /> Nevertheless, OSA in adults also implies a large scope of adverse and serious consequences,<ref name="Stranks2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Stranks EK, Crowe SF | title = The Cognitive Effects of Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An Updated Meta-analysis | journal = Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology | volume = 31 | issue = 2 | pages = 186–193 | date = March 2016 | pmid = 26743325 | doi = 10.1093/arclin/acv087 | doi-access = free }}</ref> the latter leading to higher mortality amongst OSA patients.<ref name="Robichaud-Hallé2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Robichaud-Hallé L, Beaudry M, Fortin M | title = Obstructive sleep apnea and multimorbidity | journal = BMC Pulmonary Medicine | volume = 12 | issue = 60 | pages = 60 | date = September 2012 | pmid = 23006602 | pmc = 3515504 | doi = 10.1186/1471-2466-12-60 }}</ref> Those consequences are even worsened by common morbidities such as [[obesity]].<ref name="Romero-Corral">{{cite journal | vauthors = Romero-Corral A, Caples SM, Lopez-Jimenez F, Somers VK | title = Interactions between obesity and obstructive sleep apnea: implications for treatment | journal = Chest | volume = 137 | issue = 3 | pages = 711–719 | date = March 2010 | pmid = 20202954 | pmc = 3021364 | doi = 10.1378/chest.09-0360 }}</ref>

====Neurocognitive====
Similarly to children, OSA affects [[cognition|cognitive functions]] in adults.<ref name="Alsubie" /> [[Meta-analysis]] have shown that the most common cognitive impairments happen in the domains of [[attention]], verbal and visual delayed [[long-term memory]],<ref name="Fulda2003">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fulda S, Schulz H |title=Cognitive Dysfunction in Sleep-Related Breathing Disorders: A Meta-Analysis |journal=Sleep Research Online |date=2003 |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=19–51}}</ref> visuospatial/constructional abilities and [[executive functions]],<ref name="Bucks2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bucks RS, Olaithe M, Eastwood P | title = Neurocognitive function in obstructive sleep apnoea: a meta-review | journal = Respirology | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | pages = 61–70 | date = January 2013 | pmid = 22913604 | doi = 10.1111/j.1440-1843.2012.02255.x | s2cid = 27228461 }}</ref> such as [[cognitive flexibility|mental flexibility]].<ref name="Fulda2003" /> The executive functioning – mainly dominated by the [[prefrontal cortex]]<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Nejati V, Salehinejad MA, Nitsche MA | s2cid = 207258425 | title = Interaction of the Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (l-DLPFC) and Right Orbitofrontal Cortex (OFC) in Hot and Cold Executive Functions: Evidence from Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) | journal = Neuroscience | volume = 369 | pages = 109–123 | date = January 2018 | pmid = 29113929 | doi = 10.1016/j.neuroscience.2017.10.042 }}</ref> – being significantly impaired in patients with OSA, it is believed that the prefrontal region and its connectivity are affected by sleep disorders.<ref name="Beebe2003">{{cite journal | vauthors = Beebe DW, Groesz L, Wells C, Nichols A, McGee K | title = The neuropsychological effects of obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis of norm-referenced and case-controlled data | journal = Sleep | volume = 26 | issue = 3 | pages = 298–307 | date = May 2003 | pmid = 12749549 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/26.3.298 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Regarding memory deficits, [[verbal memory]] is significantly impaired as patients show difficulties in recalling verbal information immediately as well as with a delay. While meta-analysis have shown no deficits in retention of information for patients with OSA, those impairment in verbal memory may be linked to problems in [[encoding (memory)|encoding information]].<ref name="Wallace2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Wallace A, Bucks RS | title = Memory and obstructive sleep apnea: a meta-analysis | journal = Sleep | volume = 36 | issue = 2 | pages = 203–220 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 23372268 | pmc = 3543053 | doi = 10.5665/sleep.2374 }}</ref> This deficit in encoding of information is also noticed in visuo-spatial memory; however, the [[visual memory]] seems to be intact in OSA patients.<ref name="Wallace2013" />

The cognitive impairments have been suggested to be resulting from sleep fragmentation and [[sleep deprivation]], as well as the excessive daytime sleepiness associated with them.<ref name="Bucks2012" /> More precisely, attention and memory deficits seem to result from sleep fragmentation, while deficits in global cognitive function (executive function, psychomotor function, language abilities) are more related to [[hypoxia (medical)|hypoxia]] or hypercarbia which accompanies the obstructive events during sleep.<ref name="Bucks2012" /><ref name="Olaithe2017">{{cite journal |last1=Olaithe |first1=Michelle |last2=Bucks |first2=Romola S. |last3=Hillman |first3=David R. |last4=Eastwood |first4=Peter R. |title=Cognitive deficits in obstructive sleep apnea: Insights from a meta-review and comparison with deficits observed in COPD, insomnia, and sleep deprivation |journal=Sleep Medicine Reviews |date=April 2018 |volume=38 |pages=39–49 |doi=10.1016/j.smrv.2017.03.005 |pmid=28760549 |url=https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/files/34749496/Olaithe_et_al_2017_SMRV_D_16_651R2.pdf |access-date=2023-03-17 |archive-date=2019-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190426185250/https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/files/34749496/Olaithe_et_al_2017_SMRV_D_16_651R2.pdf |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190426185250/https://api.research-repository.uwa.edu.au/files/34749496/Olaithe_et_al_2017_SMRV_D_16_651R2.pdf |date=2019-04-26 }}</ref> However, no consistent correlation has been found between the degree of cognitive impairment and the severity of the sleep disturbance or hypoxia.<ref name="Wallace2013" /><ref name="Olaithe2017" />
These impairments may improve with an effective treatment for OSA, such as [[continuous positive airway pressure]] (CPAP) therapy.<ref name="Bucks2012" /> Driving a motor vehicle is an example of a complex task that relies on driver's cognitive abilities, such as attention, reaction time and vigilance.<ref name="Rizzo2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Rizzo D | title = Driving with obstructive sleep apnea policies, behaviors and screening measures | date = August 2018 }}</ref> Very brief moments of inattention called microsleep events could be an indicator for daytime vigilance impairment, although these may not be present in all drivers with obstructive sleep apnea.<ref name="Morrone2020">{{cite journal | vauthors = Morrone E, D'Artavilla Lupo N | title = Microsleep as a marker of sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnea patients | journal = Journal of Sleep Research | volume = 29 | issue = 2 | date = 2020 | pages = e12882 | doi = 10.1111/jsr.12882 | pmid = 31180173 | s2cid = 182949124 }}</ref>

====Behavioral====
The [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|hyperactivity]] and difficulties in [[Emotional self-regulation|emotional regulation]] found in pediatric patients (children) are not reported in adults.<ref name="Alsubie" /> OSA in adults is nevertheless associated with [[personality changes]] and [[automatic behavior]].<ref name="McNicholas2008" /> The biggest impact of OSA is the excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), reported in approximately 30% of OSA patients.<ref name="Cori2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cori JM, Jackson ML, Barnes M, Westlake J, Emerson P, Lee J, Galante R, Hayley A, Wilsmore N, Kennedy GA, Howard M | display-authors = 6 | title = The Differential Effects of Regular Shift Work and Obstructive Sleep Apnea on Sleepiness, Mood and Neurocognitive Function | journal = Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine | volume = 14 | issue = 6 | pages = 941–951 | date = June 2018 | pmid = 29852909 | pmc = 5991942 | doi = 10.5664/jcsm.7156 }}</ref> EDS can be caused by the disturbance of sleep quality, the insufficient sleep duration or the sleep fragmentation<ref name="Slater2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Slater G, Steier J | title = Excessive daytime sleepiness in sleep disorders | journal = Journal of Thoracic Disease | volume = 4 | issue = 6 | pages = 608–616 | date = December 2012 | pmid = 23205286 | pmc = 3506799 | doi = 10.3978/j.issn.2072-1439.2012.10.07 }}</ref> and it is responsible for further complications as it may lead to [[depression (mood)|depressive symptoms]],<ref name="LaGrotte2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = LaGrotte C, Fernandez-Mendoza J, Calhoun SL, Liao D, Bixler EO, Vgontzas AN | title = The relative association of obstructive sleep apnea, obesity and excessive daytime sleepiness with incident depression: a longitudinal, population-based study | journal = International Journal of Obesity | volume = 40 | issue = 9 | pages = 1397–1404 | date = September 2016 | pmid = 27143032 | pmc = 5014694 | doi = 10.1038/ijo.2016.87 }}</ref> impairments of social life and decreased effectiveness at work.<ref name="Mulgrew2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Mulgrew AT, Ryan CF, Fleetham JA, Cheema R, Fox N, Koehoorn M, Fitzgerald JM, Marra C, Ayas NT | display-authors = 6 | title = The impact of obstructive sleep apnea and daytime sleepiness on work limitation | journal = Sleep Medicine | volume = 9 | issue = 1 | pages = 42–53 | date = December 2007 | pmid = 17825611 | doi = 10.1016/j.sleep.2007.01.009 }}</ref><ref name="Guilleminault2001">{{cite journal | vauthors = Guilleminault C, Brooks SN | title = Excessive daytime sleepiness: a challenge for the practising neurologist | journal = Brain | volume = 124 | issue = Pt 8 | pages = 1482–1491 | date = August 2001 | pmid = 11459741 | doi = 10.1093/brain/124.8.1482 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Studies have shown that those consequences of EDS can be improved following a CPAP treatment.<ref name="Jackson2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Jackson ML, McEvoy RD, Banks S, Barnes M | title = Neurobehavioral Impairment and CPAP Treatment Response in Mild-Moderate Obstructive Sleep Apneas | journal = Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine | volume = 14 | issue = 1 | pages = 47–56 | date = January 2018 | pmid = 29198304 | pmc = 5734892 | doi = 10.5664/jcsm.6878 }}</ref>

====Physiological====
OSA in adults is associated with a higher risk for cardiovascular morbidities, [[diabetes]], [[hypertension]], [[coronary artery disease]] and [[stroke]]<ref name="Alsubie" /><ref name="McNicholas2008" /> – OSA might have a role in the [[etiology]] of these conditions. Those conditions may lead to increased mortality<ref name="Alsubie" /><ref name="McNicholas2008" /> that an appropriate treatment for OSA may reduce.<ref name="McNicholas2008" /> OSA is often linked with hypertension as it induces an increase in [[Sympathetic nervous system|sympathetic activity]] that can lead to the elevation of blood pressure. The OSA-related [[hypercapnia]] has been suggested to be related to this development of hypertension.<ref name="Eskandari2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Eskandari D, Zou D, Grote L, Schneider H, Penzel T, Hedner J | title = Independent associations between arterial bicarbonate, apnea severity and hypertension in obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Respiratory Research | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | pages = 130 | date = June 2017 | pmid = 28659192 | pmc = 5490198 | doi = 10.1186/s12931-017-0607-9 }}</ref> Treating the OSA may prevent the development of hypertension.<ref name=Drager2013 />
The relationship between OSA and excess body weight is complex as obesity is more prevalent amongst OSA patients but can also be a [[risk factor]] for the development of OSA<ref name="McNicholas2008" /> – it accounts for 58% of adult cases.<ref name="Ashrafian2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ashrafian H, Toma T, Rowland SP, Harling L, Tan A, Efthimiou E, Darzi A, Athanasiou T | s2cid = 5284156 | display-authors = 6 | title = Bariatric Surgery or Non-Surgical Weight Loss for Obstructive Sleep Apnoea? A Systematic Review and Comparison of Meta-analyses | journal = Obesity Surgery | volume = 25 | issue = 7 | pages = 1239–1250 | date = July 2015 | pmid = 25537297 | doi = 10.1007/s11695-014-1533-2 | hdl = 10044/1/54731 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> Thus, both OSA and obesity (when present) may work synergistically and lead to [[hyperlipidemia]], diabetes, [[insulin resistance]] and other symptoms of the [[metabolic syndrome]].<ref name="Young2004" /><ref name="McNicholas2008" /> The metabolic syndrome itself is often associated with OSA: 74–85% of OSA patients are diagnosed with it. CPAP therapy can lead to an improvement of some of the cardiovascular component of the metabolic syndrome<ref name=Drager2013 /> while [[weight loss]] is also recommended for its positive effects on OSA consequences and metabolic dysfunctions.<ref name="Ashrafian2015" /><ref name="Sharma2011">{{cite journal |last1=Sharma |first1=Surendra K. |last2=Agrawal |first2=Swastik |last3=Damodaran |first3=Deepak |last4=Sreenivas |first4=Vishnubhatla |last5=Kadhiravan |first5=Tamilarasu |last6=Lakshmy |first6=Ramakrishnan |last7=Jagia |first7=Priya |last8=Kumar |first8=Atin |title=CPAP for the Metabolic Syndrome in Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |date=14 December 2011 |volume=365 |issue=24 |pages=2277–2286 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa1103944 |pmid=22168642 }}</ref> An intervention comprising exercise and diet is thus effective for the treatment of OSA as it positively impacts the severity of both obesity symptoms and OSA symptoms.<ref name="Dobrosielski2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Dobrosielski DA, Patil S, Schwartz AR, Bandeen-Roche K, Stewart KJ | title = Effects of exercise and weight loss in older adults with obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise | volume = 47 | issue = 1 | pages = 20–26 | date = January 2015 | pmid = 24870569 | pmc = 4246024 | doi = 10.1249/MSS.0000000000000387 }}</ref>

Individuals with Type 2 diabetes are often co-diagnosed with OSA, where Type 2 diabetes prevalence rates range between 15% to 30% within the OSA population.<ref name=pmid28527878>{{cite journal |last1=Reutrakul |first1=Sirimon |last2=Mokhlesi |first2=Babak |title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Diabetes |journal=Chest |date=November 2017 |volume=152 |issue=5 |pages=1070–1086 |doi=10.1016/j.chest.2017.05.009 |pmid=28527878 |pmc=5812754 }}</ref> The relationship between OSA and Type 2 diabetes could possibly be explained by the fact that OSA-characteristic fragmented sleep and irregular hypoxemia leads to the dysregulated metabolism of glucose in the blood.<ref name=pmid28527878/> In particular, many polysomnography studies showed that OSA left untreated worsens glycemic control in individuals with Type 2 diabetes.<ref name=pmid28527878/> However, it is possible that the relationship between OSA and Type 2 diabetes is bidirectional since diabetes-related nerve dysfunction may affect the respiratory system and induce breathing disturbances during sleep.<ref name=pmid28527878/>

====Psychological====
Sleep is of major importance for [[mental health|psychological and emotional health]].<ref name="Guglielmi2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Guglielmi O, Magnavita N, Garbarino S | s2cid = 4914966 | title = Sleep quality, obstructive sleep apnea, and psychological distress in truck drivers: a cross-sectional study | journal = Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology | volume = 53 | issue = 5 | pages = 531–536 | date = May 2018 | pmid = 29285594 | doi = 10.1007/s00127-017-1474-x }}</ref> As it is greatly impaired in OSA, this condition is associated with [[mood disorder]]s<ref name="Olaithe_2015" /> and several psychological outcomes,<ref name="Guglielmi2018" /> especially depression and [[anxiety disorder|anxiety]].<ref name="Garbarino2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Garbarino S, Bardwell WA, Guglielmi O, Chiorri C, Bonanni E, Magnavita N | s2cid = 53872339 | title = Association of Anxiety and Depression in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis | journal = Behavioral Sleep Medicine | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | pages = 35–57 | date = 2018 | pmid = 30453780 | doi = 10.1080/15402002.2018.1545649 }}</ref> Therefore, [[mental disorder|psychological disorders]] are commonly observed in OSA patients who show a higher [[prevalence]] of [[mental distress|psychological distress]], mostly due to the impaired sleep quality and structure and the repeated episodes of [[hypoxia (medical)|hypoxia]].<ref name="Guglielmi2018" /><ref name="Xiao2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Xiao Y, Han D, Zang H, Wang D | s2cid = 10364903 | title = The effectiveness of nasal surgery on psychological symptoms in patients with obstructive sleep apnea and nasal obstruction | journal = Acta Oto-Laryngologica | volume = 136 | issue = 6 | pages = 626–632 | date = June 2016 | pmid = 26903174 | doi = 10.3109/00016489.2016.1143120 }}</ref> The presence of psychological disorders may also worsen the sleep disorders which implies that the [[psychopathology]] may either be a [[risk factor|factor]] or a consequence of the OSA.<ref name="Garbarino2018" /> The adverse consequences of OSA such as cardiovascular comorbidities and [[metabolic disorder|metabolic disturbances]] also play a role on the development of mental disorders,<ref name="Garbarino2018" /> and patients with [[chronic condition]] have also been reported to have higher risk to experience depression.<ref name="Olaithe_2015" /> In OSA patients with psychiatric disorders, it is crucial to treat the OSA as it may reduce the psychiatric symptoms.<ref name="Gupta2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gupta MA, Simpson FC | title = Obstructive sleep apnea and psychiatric disorders: a systematic review | journal = Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine | volume = 11 | issue = 2 | pages = 165–175 | date = January 2015 | pmid = 25406268 | pmc = 4298774 | doi = 10.5664/jcsm.4466 }}</ref>

Some cases of OSA are caused by [[nasal congestion|nasal obstruction]] which has also been related to psychological problems due to an altered [[ratio]] of [[calcium]] and [[magnesium]] in [[neuron|brain cells]]. Nasal obstruction can thus aggravate the psychological health of OSA patients. Nasal surgery for those patients might decrease the OSA severity and improve the psychological symptoms.<ref name="Xiao2016" />

====Other====
Untreated OSA also leads to a decreased quality of life, difficulties in [[social skills|social functioning]],<ref name="McNicholas2008" /> occupational problems and [[work accident|accidents]]<ref name="Beebe2003" /> and a greatly increased rate of [[traffic collision|vehicle accidents]].<ref name="McNicholas2008" /><ref name="Jonas2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Jonas DE, Amick HR, Feltner C, Weber RP, Arvanitis M, Stine A, Lux L, Harris RP | s2cid = 3656829 | display-authors = 6 | title = Screening for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults: Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force | journal = JAMA | volume = 317 | issue = 4 | pages = 415–433 | date = January 2017 | pmid = 28118460 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2016.19635 }}</ref><ref name="Charokopos2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Charokopos A, Card ME, Gunderson C, Steffens C, Bastian LA | s2cid = 52182664 | title = The Association of Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Pain Outcomes in Adults: A Systematic Review | journal = Pain Medicine | volume = 19 | issue = suppl_1 | pages = S69–S75 | date = September 2018 | pmid = 30203008 | doi = 10.1093/pm/pny140 }}</ref> Those serious outcomes of OSA are mostly related to the excessive daytime sleepiness resulting from the sleep fragmentation and highlight the need to provide the patients with appropriate treatment.<ref name="McNicholas2008" /> Effective treatment majorly improves those adverse consequences, including quality of life.<ref name="McNicholas2008" />

People also frequently report [[pain disorder]]s such as [[headache]] or [[fibromyalgia]], OSA patients showing an increased pain intensity alongside a decreased [[pain tolerance]].<ref name="Charokopos2018" />

==Risk factors==

=== Obesity ===
It is well known that children, adolescents or adults with OSA are often [[obese]]. Obese people show an increase in neck fat tissue which potentiate respiratory obstruction during sleep.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schwab RJ, Kim C, Bagchi S, Keenan BT, Comyn FL, Wang S, Tapia IE, Huang S, Traylor J, Torigian DA, Bradford RM, Marcus CL | display-authors = 6 | title = Understanding the anatomic basis for obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in adolescents | journal = American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine | volume = 191 | issue = 11 | pages = 1295–1309 | date = June 2015 | pmid = 25835282 | pmc = 4476519 | doi = 10.1164/rccm.201501-0169OC }}</ref>

However, people of all ages and sex with normal body mass indices (BMIs) can also demonstrate OSA – and these people do not have significant measures of subdermal or intra neck fat as shown on [[Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry|DEXA]] scans. It is speculated that they may have increased muscle mass, or alternatively have a tendency to decreased muscle tone potentiating airway collapse during sleep.{{citation needed|date=September 2021}}

However, loss of muscle tone is a key feature of deep sleep anyway, and whilst obesity seems a common association, it is not an invariable state of OSA.

Sleeping supine (on one's back) is also represented as a risk factor for OSA. Clearly, gravity and loss of tongue and throat tone as a person enters deep sleep are clear and obvious factors contributing to OSA developing. But this explanation is also confounded by the presence of neck obesity.

Use of CPAP definitively primarily expands a collapsed upper airway, allowing for nasal breathing – and positive use of CPAP would prove that airway collapse is the cause of OSA.

Throat lesions, particularly enlarged tonsils, are well recognized as aggravators of OSA, and removal may provide full or partial or semi-permanent relief from OSA, which also indicates that enlarged tonsils may play a role in the pathogenesis of OSA.

===Age===
Old age is often accompanied by muscular and neurological loss of muscle tone of the upper airway. Decreased muscle tone is also temporarily caused by chemical depressants; alcoholic drinks and sedative medications being the most common. Permanent premature muscular tonal loss in the upper airway may be precipitated by [[traumatic brain injury]], [[neuromuscular disorders]], or poor adherence to chemical and or speech therapy treatments.

=== Muscle tone ===
Individuals with decreased muscle tone and increased soft tissue around the airway, and structural features that give rise to a narrowed airway are at high risk for OSA. Men, in which the anatomy is typified by increased mass in the torso and neck, are at increased risk of developing sleep apnea, especially through middle age and later.  Typically, women experience this condition less frequently and to a lesser degree than do men, owing partially to physiology, but possibly also to differential levels of [[progesterone]].  Prevalence in [[menopause|post-menopausal]] women approaches that of men in the same age range. Women are at greater risk for developing OSA during [[pregnancy]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Edwards N, Sullivan CE |title=Sleep-Disordered Breathing in Pregnancy |year=2008 |journal=Sleep Medicine Clinics |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=81–95 |doi=10.1016/j.jsmc.2007.10.010 |pmid=12037233 |pmc=1746354 }}</ref>

=== Lifestyle ===
Lifestyle factors such as smoking increase the risk.<ref name="Young2004" /> The effects are reversible with the stopping smoking.<ref name="Young2004" /> Children exposed to cigarette smoke may also develop OSA as the lymphadenoid tissue will proliferate excessively in contact with the irritants.<ref name="Dayyat2008" /> Alcohol, sedatives, and other medication that increase sleepiness may worse then condition.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sleep apnea – Symptoms and causes |url=https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/sleep-apnea/symptoms-causes/syc-20377631 |website=Mayo Clinic |access-date=2023-03-17 |archive-date=2017-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170923052520/http://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/sleep-apnea/basics/risk-factors/con-20020286 |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170923052520/http://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/sleep-apnea/basics/risk-factors/con-20020286 |date=2017-09-23 }}</ref> Allergic rhinitis and asthma have also been shown to increase OSA.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lu LR, Peat JK, Sullivan CE | title = Snoring in preschool children: prevalence and association with nocturnal cough and asthma | journal = Chest | volume = 124 | issue = 2 | pages = 587–593 | date = August 2003 | pmid = 12907547 | doi = 10.1378/chest.124.2.587 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=McColley |first1=Susanna A. |last2=Carroll |first2=John L. |last3=Curtis |first3=Shelly |last4=Loughlin |first4=Gerald M. |last5=Sampson |first5=Hugh A. |title=High Prevalence of Allergic Sensitization in Children With Habitual Snoring and Obstructive Sleep Apnea |journal=Chest |date=January 1997 |volume=111 |issue=1 |pages=170–173 |doi=10.1378/chest.111.1.170 |pmid=8996012 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Genetic ===
OSA also appears to have a genetic component; those with a family history of it are more likely to develop it themselves.

===Craniofacial syndromes===
One idea is that there is a general tendency towards developing short lower jaws ([[neoteny]]) is a major cause of OSA through a combined condition called [[glossoptosis]]. The posterior “normal” tongue is displaced backwards by a smaller “abnormal” anterior tongue and lower jaw. In much the same way, a narrow upper jaw will also contribute to OSA due to its relation to airway volume. A more narrow upper jaw results in more narrow nasal passages and a more narrow throat, this also appears to be why so many OSA patients experience nasal congestion especially while lying down.

[[Oral and maxillofacial surgery|Maxillofacial surgeon]]s see many effects of small lower jaws, including crowded teeth, malocclusions, as well as OSA – all of which are treatable by surgical operations that increase and normalise jaw size. Operations such as custom BIMAX, GenioPaully, and IMDO (in adolescence) offer a valid medical option that replaces all traditional forms of OSA treatment – including [[Continuous positive airway pressure|CPAP]], [[Mandibular advancement splint|Mandibular Advancement Splints]], [[tonsillectomy]] and [[Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty|UPPP]]. There are patterns of unusual facial features that occur in recognizable syndromes. Some of these craniofacial syndromes are genetic, others are from unknown causes. In many craniofacial syndromes, the features that are unusual involve the nose, mouth, and jaw, or resting muscle tone, and put the individual at risk for OSA syndrome.

[[Down syndrome]] is one such syndrome. In this [[chromosome|chromosomal]] abnormality, several features combine to make the presence of obstructive sleep apnea more likely. The specific features of Down syndrome that predispose to obstructive sleep apnea include relatively low muscle tone, narrow [[nasopharynx]], and large tongue. Obesity and enlarged tonsils and adenoids, conditions that occur commonly in the western population, are much more likely to be obstructive in a person with these features than without them. Obstructive sleep apnea does occur even more frequently in people with Down syndrome than in the general population. A little over 50% of all people with Down syndrome experience obstructive sleep apnea,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = de Miguel-Díez J, Villa-Asensi JR, Alvarez-Sala JL | title = Prevalence of sleep-disordered breathing in children with Down syndrome: polygraphic findings in 108 children | journal = Sleep | volume = 26 | issue = 8 | pages = 1006–1009 | date = December 2003 | pmid = 14746382 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/26.8.1006 }}</ref> and some physicians advocate routine testing of this group.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Shott SR, Amin R, Chini B, Heubi C, Hotze S, Akers R | title = Obstructive sleep apnea: Should all children with Down syndrome be tested? | journal = Archives of Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery | volume = 132 | issue = 4 | pages = 432–436 | date = April 2006 | pmid = 16618913 | doi = 10.1001/archotol.132.4.432 }}</ref>

In other craniofacial syndromes, the abnormal feature may actually improve the airway, but its correction may put the person at risk for obstructive sleep apnea ''after'' surgery when it is modified. [[Cleft lip and cleft palate|Cleft palate]] syndromes are such an example. During the newborn period, all humans are [[obligate nasal breathing|obligate nasal breathers]]. The palate is both the roof of the mouth and the floor of the nose. Having an open palate may make feeding difficult, but generally, does not interfere with breathing, in fact, if the nose is very obstructed, then an open palate may relieve breathing. There are a number of clefting syndromes in which the open palate is not the only abnormal feature; additionally, there is a narrow nasal passage – which may not be obvious. In such individuals, closure of the cleft palate – whether by surgery or by a temporary oral appliance – can cause the onset of obstruction.

Skeletal advancement in an effort to physically increase the [[human pharynx|pharyngeal]] airspace is often an option for craniofacial patients with upper airway obstruction and small lower jaws ([[Mandible|mandible]]s). These syndromes include [[Treacher Collins syndrome]] and [[Pierre Robin sequence]]. [[Orthognathic surgery|Mandibular advancement surgery]] is one of the modifications needed to improve the airway, others may include reduction of the tongue, [[tonsillectomy]] or modified [[uvulopalatoplasty]].{{citation needed|date=September 2020}}

=== After surgery ===
OSA can also occur as a serious post-operative complication that seems to be most frequently associated with [[pharyngeal flap surgery]] as compared to other procedures for the treatment of [[velopharyngeal inadequacy]] (VPI).<ref name=Sloan>{{cite journal |last1=Sloan |first1=Gerald M. |title=Posterior Pharyngeal Flap and Sphincter Pharyngoplasty: The State of the Art |journal=The Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Journal |date=March 2000 |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=112–122 |doi=10.1597/1545-1569_2000_037_0112_ppfasp_2.3.co_2 |pmid=10749049 |s2cid=208150617 }}</ref> In OSA, recurrent interruptions of [[Respiration (physiology)|respiration]] during sleep are associated with temporary [[airway obstruction]]. Following pharyngeal flap surgery, depending on size and position, the flap itself may have an "[[wikt:obturator|obturator]]" or obstructive effect within the [[human pharynx|pharynx]] during sleep, blocking ports of airflow and hindering effective [[Respiration (physiology)|respiration]].<ref name=Pugh>Pugh, M.B. et al. (2000). Apnea. ''Stedman's Medical Dictionary (27th ed.)'' Retrieved June 18, 2006 from STAT!Ref Online Medical Library database.{{page needed|date=May 2013}}</ref><ref name=Liao2004>{{cite journal | vauthors = Liao YF, Noordhoff MS, Huang CS, Chen PK, Chen NH, Yun C, Chuang ML | s2cid = 20976608 | title = Comparison of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in children with cleft palate following Furlow palatoplasty or pharyngeal flap for velopharyngeal insufficiency | journal = The Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Journal | volume = 41 | issue = 2 | pages = 152–156 | date = March 2004 | pmid = 14989690 | doi = 10.1597/02-162 }}</ref> There have been documented instances of severe airway obstruction, and reports of post-operative OSA continues to increase as healthcare professionals (i.e. physicians, [[Speech–language pathology|speech language pathologists]]) become more educated about this possible dangerous condition.<ref name=PetersonFalzone>{{cite book | last1 = McWilliams | first1 = Betty Jane | last2 = Peterson-Falzone | first2 = Sally J. | last3 = Hardin-Jones | first3 = Mary A. | last4 = Karnell | first4 = Michael P. | name-list-style = vanc |title=Cleft palate speech |url=https://archive.org/details/cleftpalatespeec03edpete |url-access=registration |publisher=Mosby |location=St. Louis |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8151-3153-3 |edition=3rd}}{{page needed|date=May 2013}}</ref> Subsequently, in clinical practice, concerns of OSA have matched or exceeded interest in speech outcomes following pharyngeal flap surgery.{{citation needed|date=May 2013}}

The surgical treatment for velopalatal insufficiency may cause obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. When velopalatal insufficiency is present, air leaks into the nasopharynx even when the soft palate should close off the nose. A simple test for this condition can be made by placing a tiny mirror on the nose, and asking the subject to say "P". This p sound, a plosive, is normally produced with the nasal airway closes off – all air comes out of the pursed lips, none from the nose. If it is impossible to say the sound without fogging a nasal mirror, there is an air leak – reasonable evidence of poor palatal closure. Speech is often unclear due to inability to pronounce certain sounds. One of the surgical treatments for velopalatal insufficiency involves tailoring the tissue from the back of the throat and using it to purposefully cause partial obstruction of the opening of the [[nasopharynx]]. This may actually ''cause'' OSA syndrome in susceptible individuals, particularly in the days following surgery, when swelling occurs (see below: Special Situation: Anesthesia and Surgery).{{citation needed|date=September 2020}}

Finally, patients with OSA are at an increased risk of many perioperative complications when they are present for surgery, even if the planned procedure is not on the head and neck. Guidelines intended to reduce the risk of perioperative complications have been published.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gross JB, Bachenberg KL, Benumof JL, Caplan RA, Connis RT, Coté CJ, Nickinovich DG, Prachand V, Ward DS, Weaver EM, Ydens L, Yu S | display-authors = 6 | title = Practice guidelines for the perioperative management of patients with obstructive sleep apnea: a report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Perioperative Management of patients with obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Anesthesiology | volume = 104 | issue = 5 | pages = 1081–1093; quiz 1117–1118 | date = May 2006 | pmid = 16645462 | doi = 10.1097/00000542-200605000-00026 | s2cid = 14151958 }}</ref>

==Pathophysiology==
The transition from wakefulness to sleep (either REM sleep or NREM sleep) is associated with a reduction in upper-airway muscle tone. During REM sleep, muscle tone of the throat and neck, as well as that of the vast majority of skeletal muscles, are almost completely relaxed. This allows the tongue and soft palate/oropharynx to relax, reducing airway patency and potentially impeding or completely obstructing the flow of air into the lungs during inspiration, resulting in reduced respiratory ventilation. If reductions in ventilation are associated with sufficiently low blood-oxygen levels or with sufficiently high breathing efforts against an obstructed airway, neurological mechanisms may trigger a sudden interruption of sleep, called a neurological arousal. This arousal can cause an individual to gasp for air and awaken.<ref>{{Cite journal |doi=10.1097/MED.0000000000000511 |pmid=31644470|title=Impact of circadian rhythms on female reproduction and infertility treatment success |year=2019 |last1=Mills |first1=Jacqueline |last2=Kuohung |first2=Wendy |journal=Current Opinion in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Obesity |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=317–321 |s2cid=204865937 }}</ref> These arousals rarely result in complete awakening but can have a significant negative effect on the restorative quality of sleep. In significant cases of OSA, one consequence is [[sleep deprivation]] resulting from the repetitive disruption and recovery of sleep activity. This sleep interruption in Stage 3 (also called [[slow-wave sleep]]), and in REM sleep, can interfere with normal growth patterns, [[healing]] and [[immune response]], especially in children and young adults.

The fundamental cause of OSA is a blocked upper airway, usually behind the tongue and epiglottis, whereby the otherwise patent airway, in an erect and awake patient, collapses when the patient is lying on his or her back and loses muscle tone upon entering deep sleep.

At the beginning of sleep, a patient is in light sleep and there is no tone loss of throat muscles. Airflow is laminar and soundless. As the upper airway collapse progresses, the obstruction becomes increasingly apparent by the initiation of noisy breathing as air turbulence increases, followed by gradually louder [[snoring]] as a [[Venturi effect]] forms through the ever-narrowing air passage.

The patient's blood-oxygen saturation gradually falls until cessation of sleep noises, signifying total airway obstruction of airflow, which may last for several minutes.

Eventually, the patient must at least partially awaken from deep sleep into light sleep, automatically regaining general muscle tone. This switch from deep to light to deep sleep can be recorded using [[Emission computed tomography|ECT]] monitors.

In light sleep, muscle tone is near normal, the airway spontaneously opens, normal noiseless breathing resumes and blood-oxygen saturation rises. Eventually, the patient reenters deep sleep, upper airway tone is again lost, the patient enters the various levels of noisy breathing and the airway blockage returns.

The cycle of muscle-tone loss and restoration coinciding with periods of deep and light sleep repeats throughout the patient's period of sleep.

The number of apnoea and hypopnoea episodes during any given hour is counted and given a score. If a patient has an average of five or more episodes per hour, mild OSA may be confirmed. An average of 30 or more episodes per hour indicates severe OSA.

===Models===
The causes of spontaneous upper-airway blockage are strongly debated. The areas of thought are divided mostly into three medical groups.

Some [[Pulmonology|pulmonologists]] and [[Neurology|neurologists]] believe the risk factors to be:
* Advanced age, although OSA occurs in neonates, as with [[Pierre Robin sequence|Pierre Robin]] syndrome, and in all age groups of people.
* Brain injury (temporary or permanent), although this does not account for the 99% of OSA patients who have normal brains and normal lives.
* Decreased muscle tone caused by drugs or alcohol, or caused by neurological disorders. This also would not account for the majority of people with OSA.
* Long-term snoring, which is postulated to potentially induce local nerve lesions in the soft tissues of the [[pharynx]]. Snoring may produce traumatic vibrations that may give rise to nerve injuries in the upper airway muscles, further contributing to OSA.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Saboisky JP, Butler JE, Gandevia SC, Eckert DJ | title = Functional role of neural injury in obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Frontiers in Neurology | volume = 3 | pages = 95 | date = 15 June 2012 | pmid = 22715333 | pmc = 3375463 | doi = 10.3389/fneur.2012.00095 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* Increased soft tissue around the airway, often resulting from obesity, though not seen in all patients with OSA.

Some [[Otorhinolaryngology|otorhinolaryngologists]] believe the risk factors to be structural features that give rise to a narrowed airway, such as enlarged [[tonsils]], an enlarged posterior tongue or fat deposits in the neck. Further factors leading to OSA can be impaired nasal breathing, floppy soft palate or a collapsible [[epiglottis]].

Some [[Oral and maxillofacial surgery|oral and maxillofacial surgeons]] believe the risk factors to be a number of primary forms of [[Micrognathism|mandibular hypoplasia]], which offers a primary anatomical basis to the development of OSA through [[glossoptosis]]. Some maxillofacial surgeons who offer [[Orthognathic surgery|orthognathic]] surgery for treatment of OSA believe that their treatments offer superior guarantees of cure of OSA.

==Diagnosis==
The [[United States Preventive Services Task Force]] in 2017 concluded that there was uncertainty about the accuracy or utility of all potential screening tools for OSA,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jonas DE, Amick HR, Feltner C, Weber RP, Arvanitis M, Stine A, Lux L, Harris RP | display-authors = 6 | title = Screening for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults: Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force | journal = JAMA | volume = 317 | issue = 4 | pages = 415–433 | date = January 2017 | pmid = 28118460 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2016.19635 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and recommended that evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening in asymptomatic adults.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bibbins-Domingo K, Grossman DC, Curry SJ, Davidson KW, Epling JW, García FA, Herzstein J, Kemper AR, Krist AH, Kurth AE, Landefeld CS, Mangione CM, Phillips WR, Phipps MG, Pignone MP, Silverstein M, Tseng CW | display-authors = 6 | title = Screening for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement | journal = JAMA | volume = 317 | issue = 4 | pages = 407–414 | date = January 2017 | pmid = 28118461 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2016.20325 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

The diagnosis of OSA syndrome is made when the patient shows recurrent episodes of partial or complete collapse of the upper airway during sleep resulting in apneas or hypopneas, respectively.<ref name="Obstructive sleep apnea is a common">{{cite journal | vauthors = Franklin KA, Lindberg E | title = Obstructive sleep apnea is a common disorder in the population-a review on the epidemiology of sleep apnea | journal = Journal of Thoracic Disease | volume = 7 | issue = 8 | pages = 1311–1322 | date = August 2015 | pmid = 26380759 | pmc = 4561280 | doi = 10.3978/j.issn.2072-1439.2015.06.11 }}</ref> Criteria defining an apnea or a hypopnea vary. The [[American Academy of Sleep Medicine|American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM)]] defines an apnea as a reduction in airflow of ≥&thinsp;90% lasting at least 10 seconds. A hypopnea is defined as a reduction in airflow of ≥&thinsp;30% lasting at least 10 seconds and associated with a ≥&thinsp;4% decrease in pulse oxygenation, or as a ≥&thinsp;30% reduction in airflow lasting at least 10 seconds and associated either with a ≥&thinsp;3% decrease in pulse oxygenation or with an arousal.<ref>Berry RB, Quan SF, Abrue AR, et al.; for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. The AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events: Rules, Terminology and Technical Specifications. Version 2.6. Darien, IL: American Academy of Sleep Medicine; 2020.</ref>

To define the severity of the condition, the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) or the Respiratory Disturbance Index (RDI) are used. While the AHI measures the mean number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep, the RDI adds to this measure the respiratory effort-related arousals (RERAs).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kapur VK, Auckley DH, Chowdhuri S, Kuhlmann DC, Mehra R, Ramar K, Harrod CG | title = Clinical Practice Guideline for Diagnostic Testing for Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline | journal = Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine | volume = 13 | issue = 3 | pages = 479–504 | date = March 2017 | pmid = 28162150 | pmc = 5337595 | doi = 10.5664/jcsm.6506 }}</ref> The OSA syndrome is thus diagnosed if the AHI is >&thinsp;5 episodes per hour and results in daytime sleepiness and fatigue or when the RDI is ≥&thinsp;15 independently of the symptoms.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Thurnheer |first1=R. |title=Diagnosis of the obstructive sleep apnea syndrome |journal=Minerva Pneumologica |date=September 2007 |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=191–204 |url=https://www.minervamedica.it/en/journals/minerva-pneumologica/article.php?cod=R16Y2007N03A0191 |s2cid=52540419 |access-date=2023-03-17 |archive-date=2020-10-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201023215006/https://www.minervamedica.it/en/journals/minerva-pneumologica/article.php?cod=R16Y2007N03A0191 |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201023215006/https://www.minervamedica.it/en/journals/minerva-pneumologica/article.php?cod=R16Y2007N03A0191 |date=2020-10-23 }}</ref> According to the American Association of Sleep Medicine, daytime sleepiness is determined as mild, moderate and severe depending on its impact on social life. Daytime sleepiness can be assessed with the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), a self-reported questionnaire on the propensity to fall asleep or doze off during daytime.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Crook S, Sievi NA, Bloch KE, Stradling JR, Frei A, Puhan MA, Kohler M | title = Minimum important difference of the Epworth Sleepiness Scale in obstructive sleep apnoea: estimation from three randomised controlled trials | journal = Thorax | volume = 74 | issue = 4 | pages = 390–396 | date = April 2019 | pmid = 30100576 | doi = 10.1136/thoraxjnl-2018-211959 | s2cid = 51967356 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Screening tools for OSA itself comprise the STOP questionnaire, the Berlin questionnaire and the STOP-BANG questionnaire which has been reported as being a very powerful tool to detect OSA.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chiu HY, Chen PY, Chuang LP, Chen NH, Tu YK, Hsieh YJ, Wang YC, Guilleminault C | display-authors = 6 | title = Diagnostic accuracy of the Berlin questionnaire, STOP-BANG, STOP, and Epworth sleepiness scale in detecting obstructive sleep apnea: A bivariate meta-analysis | journal = Sleep Medicine Reviews | volume = 36 | pages = 57–70 | date = December 2017 | pmid = 27919588 | doi = 10.1016/j.smrv.2016.10.004 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Amra B, Javani M, Soltaninejad F, Penzel T, Fietze I, Schoebel C, Farajzadegan Z | title = Comparison of Berlin Questionnaire, STOP-Bang, and Epworth Sleepiness Scale for Diagnosing Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Persian Patients | journal = International Journal of Preventive Medicine | volume = 9 | issue =
