28 | pages = 28 | date = 2018 | pmid = 29619152 | pmc = 5869953 | doi = 10.4103/ijpvm.IJPVM_131_17 }}</ref>  A high Mallampati score (class 3 or 4) is associated with a higher incidence of sleep apnea.<ref name="mallampati">{{cite journal |last1=Nuckton |first1=Thomas J. |last2=Glidden |first2=David V. |last3=Browner |first3=Warren S. |last4=Claman |first4=David M. |title=Physical Examination: Mallampati Score as an Independent Predictor of Obstructive Sleep Apnea |journal=Sleep |date=July 2006 |volume=29 |issue=7 |pages=903–908 |doi=10.1093/sleep/29.7.903 |url=https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/29/7/903/2708391 |access-date=19 March 2023 |archive-date=23 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220223222352/https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/29/7/903/2708391 |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220223222352/https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/29/7/903/2708391 |date=23 February 2022 }}</ref>

===Classification===
In the third edition of the [[International Classification of Sleep Disorders]] (ICSD-3), obstructive sleep apnea is classified amongst the sleep-related breathing disorders and is divided in two categories, namely adult OSA and pediatric OSA.<ref name=AASM3rd>{{cite book |last1=American Academy of Sleep Medicine |title=International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition |date=2014 |publisher=American Academy of Sleep Medicine |location=Darien, IL}}</ref> Obstructive sleep apnea is differentiated from [[central sleep apnea]] (CSA), which is characterized by episodes of reduction or cessation in breathing attributable to decreased effort, rather than upper airway obstruction.<ref name=Tung2017>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tung P, Levitzky YS, Wang R, Weng J, Quan SF, Gottlieb DJ, Rueschman M, Punjabi NM, Mehra R, Bertisch S, Benjamin EJ, Redline S | display-authors = 6 | title = Obstructive and Central Sleep Apnea and the Risk of Incident Atrial Fibrillation in a Community Cohort of Men and Women | journal = Journal of the American Heart Association | volume = 6 | issue = 7 | date = July 2017 | pmid = 28668820 | pmc = 5586257 | doi = 10.1161/jaha.116.004500 }}</ref> The respiratory effort must then be assessed in order to correctly classify the apnea as obstructive given the specificity of the diaphragmatic activity in this condition:<ref name=Stoohs2005>{{cite journal | vauthors = Stoohs RA, Blum HC, Knaack L, Butsch-von-der-Heydt B, Guilleminault C | title = Comparison of pleural pressure and transcutaneous diaphragmatic electromyogram in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome | journal = Sleep | volume = 28 | issue = 3 | pages = 321–329 | date = March 2005 | pmid = 16173653 }}</ref> the inspiratory effort is continued or increased through the entire episode of absent airflow.<ref name=AASMManual>{{cite web |last1=American Academy of Sleep Medicine |title=AASM Practice Guidelines |url=https://aasm.org/clinical-resources/practice-standards/practice-guidelines/ |website=AASM |access-date=19 June 2019 |archive-date=18 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190618131459/https://aasm.org/clinical-resources/practice-standards/practice-guidelines/ |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190618131459/https://aasm.org/clinical-resources/practice-standards/practice-guidelines/ |date=18 June 2019 }}</ref>

When [[hypopnea]]s are present alongside apneas, the term obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea is used and when it is associated with daytime sleepiness and other daytime symptoms, it is called obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mbata |first1=GC |last2=Chukwuka |first2=JC |title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea Hypopnea Syndrome |journal=Annals of Medical and Health Sciences Research |date=2012 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=74–77 |doi=10.4103/2141-9248.96943 |pmid=23209996 |pmc=3507119 }}</ref> To be categorized as obstructive, the hypopnea must meet one or more of the following symptoms: (1) [[snoring]] during the event, (2) increased oronasal flow flattening, or (3) [[Diaphragmatic paradox|thoraco-abdominal paradoxical respiration]] during the event.<ref name=AASMManual /> If none of them are present during the event, then it is categorized as central hypopnea.

===Criteria===
According to the [[International Classification of Sleep Disorders]], there are 4 types of criteria. The first one concerns sleep – excessive sleepiness, nonrestorative sleep, fatigue or insomnia symptoms. The second and third criteria are about respiration – waking with breath holding, gasping, or choking; snoring, breathing interruptions or both during sleep. The last criterion revolved around medical issues as hypertension, coronary artery disease, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, mood disorder or cognitive impairment. Two levels of severity are distinguished, the first one is determined by a polysomnography or home sleep apnea test demonstrating 5 or more predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour of sleep and the higher levels are determined by 15 or more events. If the events are present less than 5 times per hour, no obstructive sleep apnea is diagnosed.<ref>American Academy of Sleep Medicine. International classification of sleep disorders. 3rd ed. Darien, IL: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 2014.{{page needed|date=September 2020}}</ref>

A considerable night-to-night variability further complicates diagnosis of OSA. In unclear cases, multiple testing might be required to achieve an accurate diagnosis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tschopp|first1=Samuel|last2=Wimmer|first2=Wilhelm|last3=Caversaccio|first3=Marco|last4=Borner|first4=Urs|last5=Tschopp|first5=Kurt|date=2021-03-30|title=Night-to-night variability in obstructive sleep apnea using peripheral arterial tonometry: a case for multiple night testing|journal=Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine|volume=17|issue=9|language=en|pages=1751–1758|doi=10.5664/jcsm.9300|pmid=33783347|pmc=8636340|s2cid=232420123|issn=1550-9389}}</ref>

===Sleep study===
{| class="wikitable" align="right" style="margin: 1em 1em "
! [[Apnea–hypopnea index|AHI]]||Rating
|-
| <&thinsp;5||Normal
|-
| 5–15||Mild
|-
| 15–30||Moderate
|-
| >&thinsp;30||Severe
|}

<!-- Deleted image removed: [[Image:Apnea2Min.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Two minute epoch representing continuous OSA. Click on this image for larger version.]] -->
Nighttime in-laboratory Level 1 [[polysomnography]] (PSG) is the gold standard test for diagnosis. Patients are monitored with EEG leads, [[pulse oximetry]], temperature and pressure sensors to detect nasal and oral airflow, respiratory impedance plethysmography or similar resistance belts around the chest and abdomen to detect motion, an ECG lead, and EMG sensors to detect muscle contraction in the chin, chest, and legs. A hypopnea can be based on one of two criteria. It can either be a reduction in airflow of at least 30% for more than 10 seconds associated with at least 4% oxygen desaturation or a reduction in airflow of at least 30% for more than 10 seconds associated with at least 3% oxygen desaturation or an arousal from sleep on EEG.<ref name=stats>{{cite journal |authors=Jennifer M. Slowik, Jacob F. Collen| title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea |date=2020 |journal=StatPearls |pmid=29083619}} {{CC-notice|cc=by4|url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459252/}}</ref>

An "event" can be either an apnea, characterized by complete cessation of airflow for at least 10 seconds, or a [[hypopnea]] in which airflow decreases by 50 percent for 10 seconds or decreases by 30 percent if there is an associated decrease in the oxygen saturation or an arousal from sleep.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Sleep-related breathing disorders in adults: recommendations for syndrome definition and measurement techniques in clinical research. The Report of an American Academy of Sleep Medicine Task Force | journal = Sleep | volume = 22 | issue = 5 | pages = 667–689 | date = August 1999 | pmid = 10450601 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/22.5.667 | doi-access = free }}</ref> To grade the severity of sleep apnea, the number of events per hour is reported as the [[apnea-hypopnea index]] (AHI). An AHI of less than 5 is considered normal. An AHI of 5–15 is mild; 15–30 is moderate, and more than 30 events per hour characterizes severe sleep apnea.

===Home oximetry===
In people who are at high likelihood of OSA, home [[oximetry]] (a non-invasive method of monitoring blood oxygenation) may be adequate and easier to obtain than formal polysomnography.<ref name="pmid17283346">{{cite journal | vauthors = Mulgrew AT, Fox N, Ayas NT, Ryan CF | s2cid = 25693423 | title = Diagnosis and initial management of obstructive sleep apnea without polysomnography: a randomized validation study | journal = Annals of Internal Medicine | volume = 146 | issue = 3 | pages = 157–166 | date = February 2007 | pmid = 17283346 | doi = 10.7326/0003-4819-146-3-200702060-00004 }}</ref> High probability patients were identified by an [[Epworth Sleepiness Scale]] (ESS) score of 10 or greater and a Sleep Apnea Clinical Score (SACS) of 15 or greater.<ref name="pmid7952553">{{cite journal | vauthors = Flemons WW, Whitelaw WA, Brant R, Remmers JE | title = Likelihood ratios for a sleep apnea clinical prediction rule | journal = American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine | volume = 150 | issue = 5 Pt 1 | pages = 1279–1285 | date = November 1994 | pmid = 7952553 | doi = 10.1164/ajrccm.150.5.7952553 }}</ref> Home oximetry, however, does not measure apneic events or respiratory event-related arousals and thus does not produce an AHI value.

==Treatment ==
[[File:CPAP.png |thumb|upright=1.3|Person with a CPAP machine]]
The treatment depends upon the level of obstruction, if the obstruction is at nose or epiglottis surgery could be required. Numerous treatment options are used.<ref name="Friedman2008">Friedman: Sleep Apnea and Snoring, 1st ed. 2008</ref> Avoiding alcohol and smoking is recommended,<ref name=Aza2012>{{cite journal | vauthors = Azagra-Calero E, Espinar-Escalona E, Barrera-Mora JM, Llamas-Carreras JM, Solano-Reina E | title = Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS). Review of the literature | journal = Medicina Oral, Patologia Oral y Cirugia Bucal | volume = 17 | issue = 6 | pages = e925–929 | date = November 2012 | pmid = 22549673 | pmc = 3505711 | doi = 10.4317/medoral.17706 }}</ref> as is avoiding medications that relax the central nervous system (for example, sedatives and muscle relaxants). [[Weight loss]] is recommended in those who are [[overweight]]. [[Continuous positive airway pressure]] (CPAP) and [[mandibular advancement device]]s are often used and found to be equally effective.<ref name=Qa2013/><ref name=Brat2015>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bratton DJ, Gaisl T, Wons AM, Kohler M | title = CPAP vs Mandibular Advancement Devices and Blood Pressure in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis | journal = JAMA | volume = 314 | issue = 21 | pages = 2280–2293 | date = December 2015 | pmid = 26624827 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2015.16303 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Physical training, even without weight loss, improves sleep apnea.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Iftikhar IH, Kline CE, Youngstedt SD | title = Effects of exercise training on sleep apnea: a meta-analysis | journal = Lung | volume = 192 | issue = 1 | pages = 175–184 | date = February 2014 | pmid = 24077936 | pmc = 4216726 | doi = 10.1007/s00408-013-9511-3 }}</ref> There is insufficient evidence to support widespread use of medications.<ref name=Qa2013/> In selected patients, e.g. with tonsillar hyperplasia tonsillectomy is recommended. In patients failing CPAP and oral appliances, surgical treatment with conservative uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) as [[salvage surgery]] is recommended. Randomized controlled studies of the efficacy of UPPP are published, showing effect on nocturnal respiration and excessive daytime sleepiness,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Browaldh N, Nerfeldt P, Lysdahl M, Bring J, Friberg D | s2cid = 27682387| title = SKUP3 randomised controlled trial: polysomnographic results after uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in selected patients with obstructive sleep apnoea| journal = Thorax | volume = 68 | issue = 9 | pages = 846–853 | date = September 2013 | pmid = 23644225 | doi = 10.1136/thoraxjnl-2012-202610 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and a systematic Meta-analysis.<ref name=pmid30056286/>

=== Physical intervention ===
The most widely used treatment is ''positive airway pressure'' whereby a breathing machine pumps a controlled stream of air through a mask worn over the nose or mouth. The additional pressure holds open the airway. There are several variants:
* Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is effective for both moderate and severe disease.<ref name=Gil2006/> It is the most common treatment for obstructive sleep apnea.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Askland |first1=Kathleen |last2=Wright |first2=Lauren |last3=Wozniak |first3=Dariusz R |last4=Emmanuel |first4=Talia |last5=Caston |first5=Jessica |last6=Smith |first6=Ian |title=Educational, supportive and behavioural interventions to improve usage of continuous positive airway pressure machines in adults with obstructive sleep apnoea |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |date=7 April 2020 |volume=2020 |issue=4 |pages=CD007736 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD007736.pub3 |pmid=32255210 |pmc=7137251 }}</ref>
* [[Positive airway pressure|Variable positive airway pressure]] (VPAP) (also known as bilevel (BiPAP or BPAP)) uses an electronic circuit to monitor the patient's breathing and provides two different pressures, a higher one during [[inhalation]] and a lower pressure during [[exhalation]]. This system is more expensive and is sometimes used with patients who have other coexisting respiratory problems or who find breathing out against an increased pressure to be uncomfortable or disruptive to their sleep.
* [[Nasal EPAP]], which is a bandage-like device placed over the nostrils that utilizes a person's own breathing to create positive airway pressure to prevent obstructed breathing.<ref name=Riaz2015rev>{{cite journal | vauthors = Riaz M, Certal V, Nigam G, Abdullatif J, Zaghi S, Kushida CA, Camacho M | title = Nasal Expiratory Positive Airway Pressure Devices (Provent) for OSA: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis | journal = Sleep Disorders | volume = 2015 | pages = 734798 | date = 2015 | pmid = 26798519 | pmc = 4699057 | doi = 10.1155/2015/734798 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* Automatic positive airway pressure, also known as "Auto CPAP", incorporates pressure sensors and monitors the person's breathing.<ref  name="pmid15486338">{{cite journal |last1=Whitelaw |first1=William A. |last2=Brant |first2=Rollin F. |last3=Flemons |first3=W. Ward |title=Clinical Usefulness of Home Oximetry Compared with Polysomnography for Assessment of Sleep Apnea |journal=American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine |date=15 January 2005 |volume=171 |issue=2 |pages=188–193 |doi=10.1164/rccm.200310-1360OC |pmid=15486338 }} Review in: {{cite journal | vauthors = Caples SM | title = The accuracy of physicians in predicting successful treatment response in suspected obstructive sleep apnea did not differ between home monitoring and polysomnography | journal = ACP Journal Club | volume = 143 | issue = 1 | pages = 21 | year = 2005 | doi = 10.7326/ACPJC-2005-143-1-021 | pmid = 15989309 | s2cid = 219673066 }}</ref><ref name="pmid11902424">{{cite journal | vauthors = Littner M, Hirshkowitz M, Davila D, Anderson WM, Kushida CA, Woodson BT, Johnson SF, Merrill SW | display-authors = 6 | title = Practice parameters for the use of auto-titrating continuous positive airway pressure devices for titrating pressures and treating adult patients with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. An American Academy of Sleep Medicine report | journal = Sleep | volume = 25 | issue = 2 | pages = 143–147 | date = March 2002 | pmid = 11902424 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/25.2.143 }}</ref>
* A 5% reduction in weight among those with moderate to severe OSA may decrease symptoms similarly to CPAP.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McNicholas WT, Bonsignore MR, Lévy P, Ryan S | title = Mild obstructive sleep apnoea: clinical relevance and approaches to management | journal = The Lancet. Respiratory Medicine | volume = 4 | issue = 10 | pages = 826–834 | date = October 2016 | pmid = 27245915 | doi = 10.1016/S2213-2600(16)30146-1 }}</ref>

Encouraging people with moderate to severe OSA to use CPAP devices can be challenging as use often requires a behavioural change in sleeping habits.<ref name=":2" /> 8% of people who use CPAP devices stop using them after the first night, and 50% of people with moderate to severe OSA stop using their devices in the first year.<ref name=":2" /> Educational initiatives and supportive interventions to help improve compliance with CPAP therapy have been shown to improve the length of time people who need CPAP therapy use their devices.<ref name=":2" />

Oral appliance or splints may be preferred by patients but may not be as effective as CPAP.<ref name="Gil2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Giles TL, Lasserson TJ, Smith BH, White J, Wright J, Cates CJ | editor1-first = Tammie | editor1-last = Giles | title = Continuous positive airways pressure for obstructive sleep apnoea in adults | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | issue = 3 | pages = CD001106 | date = July 2006 | pmid = 16855960 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD001106.pub3 }}</ref> This device is a mouthguard similar to those used in sports to protect the teeth. It is designed to hold the lower jaw slightly down and forward relative to the natural, relaxed position. This position holds the tongue farther away from the back of the airway and may be enough to relieve apnea or improve breathing. Evidence to support oral appliances in children is insufficient with very low evidence of effect. They may be considered in specified cases as an auxiliary in the treatment of children who have craniofacial anomalies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Carvalho |first1=Fernando R |last2=Lentini-Oliveira |first2=Débora A |last3=Prado |first3=Lucila BF |last4=Prado |first4=Gilmar F |last5=Carvalho |first5=Luciane BC |title=Oral appliances and functional orthopaedic appliances for obstructive sleep apnoea in children |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |date=4 October 2016 |volume=10 |issue=11 |pages=CD005520 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD005520.pub3 |pmid=27701747 |pmc=6458031 }}</ref>

Many people benefit from sleeping at a ''30-degree elevation'' of the upper body<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Neill AM, Angus SM, Sajkov D, McEvoy RD | title = Effects of sleep posture on upper airway stability in patients with obstructive sleep apnea | journal = American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine | volume = 155 | issue = 1 | pages = 199–204 | date = January 1997 | pmid = 9001312 | doi = 10.1164/ajrccm.155.1.9001312 }}</ref> or higher, as if in a [[recliner]]. Doing so helps prevent the gravitational collapse of the airway. [[Human anatomical terms#Anatomical directions|Sleeping on a side]] as opposed to [[supine position|sleeping on the back]] is also recommended.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Nakano H, Ikeda T, Hayashi M, Ohshima E, Onizuka A | title = Effects of body position on snoring in apneic and nonapneic snorers | journal = Sleep | volume = 26 | issue = 2 | pages = 169–172 | date = March 2003 | pmid = 12683476 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/26.2.169 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Loord H, Hultcrantz E | s2cid = 323418 | title = Positioner--a method for preventing sleep apnea | journal = Acta Oto-Laryngologica | volume = 127 | issue = 8 | pages = 861–868 | date = August 2007 | pmid = 17762999 | doi = 10.1080/00016480601089390 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Szollosi I, Roebuck T, Thompson B, Naughton MT | title = Lateral sleeping position reduces severity of central sleep apnea / Cheyne-Stokes respiration | journal = Sleep | volume = 29 | issue = 8 | pages = 1045–1051 | date = August 2006 | pmid = 16944673 | doi = 10.1093/sleep/29.8.1045 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Some studies have suggested that ''playing a [[wind instrument]]'' may reduce snoring and apnea incidents.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Caba |first1=Justin |title=How The Saxophone Could Solve Your Sleep Apnea |url=https://www.medicaldaily.com/learning-play-wind-instrument-could-lower-your-risk-obstructive-sleep-apnea-329582 |work=Medical Daily |date=16 April 2015 |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=10 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221210013706/https://www.medicaldaily.com/learning-play-wind-instrument-could-lower-your-risk-obstructive-sleep-apnea-329582 |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221210013706/https://www.medicaldaily.com/learning-play-wind-instrument-could-lower-your-risk-obstructive-sleep-apnea-329582 |date=10 December 2022 }}</ref> This may be especially true of [[double reed instrument]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ward |first1=Christopher P. |last2=York |first2=Kaki M. |last3=McCoy |first3=John G. |title=Risk of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Lower in Double Reed Wind Musicians |journal=Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine |date=15 June 2012 |volume=08 |issue=3 |pages=251–255 |doi=10.5664/jcsm.1906 |pmid=22701381 |pmc=3365082 }}</ref>

=== Surgery ===
Surgical treatments to modify airway anatomy, known as [[sleep surgery]], are varied and must be tailored to the specific airway obstruction needs of a patient. Surgery is not considered a first line treatment for obstructive sleep apnea in adults. There are prospective, randomized, comparative clinical trials,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Browaldh |first1=Nanna |last2=Nerfeldt |first2=Pia |last3=Lysdahl |first3=Michael |last4=Bring |first4=Johan |last5=Friberg |first5=Danielle |title=SKUP3 randomised controlled trial: polysomnographic results after uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in selected patients with obstructive sleep apnoea |journal=Thorax |date=1 September 2013 |volume=68 |issue=9 |pages=846–853 |doi=10.1136/thoraxjnl-2012-202610 |pmid=23644225 |s2cid=27682387 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and also a systematic Meta-analysis,<ref name=pmid30056286>{{cite journal |last1=Stuck |first1=Boris A. |last2=Ravesloot |first2=Madeline J. L. |last3=Eschenhagen |first3=Till |last4=de Vet |first4=H. C. W. |last5=Sommer |first5=J. Ulrich |title=Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty with or without tonsillectomy in the treatment of adult obstructive sleep apnea – A systematic review |journal=Sleep Medicine |date=1 October 2018 |volume=50 |pages=152–165 |doi=10.1016/j.sleep.2018.05.004 |pmid=30056286 |s2cid=51878426 }}</ref> showing evidence that conservative [[uvulopalatopharyngoplasty]] (UPPP) with or without [[tonsillectomy]] is effective in selected patients failing conservative treatment. For those with obstructive sleep apnea unable or unwilling to comply with first line treatment, the surgical intervention has to be adapted to an individual's specific anatomy and physiology, personal preference and disease severity.<ref name="Friedman2008"/> Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty with or without is the most common surgery for patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Studies have shown that treatment effect of tonsillectomy increases with tonsil size.<ref name="onlinelibrary.wiley.com">{{Cite journal|last1=Tschopp|first1=Samuel|last2=Tschopp|first2=Kurt|date=2019|title=Tonsil size and outcome of uvulopalatopharyngoplasty with tonsillectomy in obstructive sleep apnea|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/lary.27899|journal=The Laryngoscope|language=en|volume=129|issue=12|pages=E449–E454|doi=10.1002/lary.27899|pmid=30848478|s2cid=73503702|issn=1531-4995|access-date=2023-03-17|archive-date=2021-11-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211126105456/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/lary.27899|url-status=live}} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211126105456/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/lary.27899 |date=2021-11-26 }}</ref> However, there is little randomized clinical trial evidence for other types of [[sleep surgery]].<ref name=Qa2013/>

There are a number of different operations that may be performed:

* [[Septoplasty]] is a corrective surgical procedure for [[Nasal septum deviation]] in which the [[nasal septum]] is straightened.
* [[Tonsillectomy]]<ref name="onlinelibrary.wiley.com"/> or [[adenoidectomy]] in an attempt to increase the size of the airway.
* Removal or reduction of parts of the [[soft palate]] and some or all of the [[uvula]], such as [[uvulopalatopharyngoplasty]] (UPPP) or laser-assisted uvulopalatoplasty (''LAUP''). Modern variants of this procedure sometimes use [[radiofrequency]] waves to heat and remove tissue.
* [[Turbinate reduction|Turbinectomy]] is a surgical procedure in which all or some of the [[turbinate]] bones are removed to relieve [[nasal obstruction]].
* Reduction of the tongue base, either with laser excision or [[radiofrequency ablation]].
* [[Genioglossus advancement]], in which a small portion of the lower jaw that attaches to the tongue is moved forward, to pull the tongue away from the back of the airway.
* [[Hyoid suspension]], in which the [[hyoid bone]] in the neck, another attachment point for tongue muscles, is pulled forward in front of the [[larynx]].
* [[Maxillomandibular advancement]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.umm.edu/patiented/articles/what_surgical_procedures_sleep_apnea_000065_10.htm |title=Sleep apnea |publisher=University of Maryland Medical Center |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080430151746/http://www.umm.edu/patiented/articles/what_surgical_procedures_sleep_apnea_000065_10.htm |archive-date=2008-04-30 }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080430151746/http://www.umm.edu/patiented/articles/what_surgical_procedures_sleep_apnea_000065_10.htm |date=2008-04-30 }}</ref>

In the morbidly obese, a major loss of weight (such as what occurs after [[bariatric surgery]]) can sometimes cure the condition.

OSA in children is often due to enlarged tonsils and adenoids because the lymphoid tissue grows fast during young age. Surgical removal of enlarged tonsils (tonsillectomy) and the adenoid (adenoidectomy) are first line treatment among children with OSA. The operation is a common procedure but in the most extreme cases, children with severe OSA requires special precautions before, surgery (see "Surgery and obstructive sleep apnea syndrome" below). In some countries, a milder surgical procedure called tonsillotomy is used to remove the protruding tonsillar tissue, a method associated with less pain and lower risk of postoperative hemorrhage.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Borgström |first1=Anna |last2=Nerfeldt |first2=Pia |last3=Friberg |first3=Danielle |title=Adenotonsillotomy Versus Adenotonsillectomy in Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An RCT |journal=Pediatrics |date=1 April 2017 |volume=139 |issue=4 |pages=e20163314 |doi=10.1542/peds.2016-3314 |pmid=28320866 |s2cid=23443654 }}</ref>

===Rapid palatal expansion===
{{see also|Palatal expansion}}

In children, there are orthodontic treatment to expand the volume of the nasal airway, such as nonsurgical rapid [[palatal expansion]]. Since the palatal suture is fused in adults, regular RPE using tooth-borne expanders cannot be performed. Mini-implant assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) is a non-surgical option for the transverse expansion of the maxilla in adults. This method may improve OSA measures.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abdullatif |first1=Jose |last2=Certal |first2=Victor |last3=Zaghi |first3=Soroush |last4=Song |first4=Sungjin A. |last5=Chang |first5=Edward T. |last6=Gillespie |first6=M. Boyd |last7=Camacho |first7=Macario |title=Maxillary expansion and maxillomandibular expansion for adult OSA: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=Journal of Cranio-Maxillofacial Surgery |date=1 May 2016 |volume=44 |issue=5 |pages=574–578 |doi=10.1016/j.jcms.2016.02.001 |pmid=26948172 }}</ref>

=== Neurostimulation ===
For people who cannot use a positive airway pressure device, in the USA in 2014 pre-market approval was given to upper airway stimulation system that senses respiration and delivers mild electrical stimulation to the [[hypoglossal nerve]] to increase muscle tone at the back of the tongue. The device includes a handheld controller to allow it to be switched on before sleep and is powered by an implantable pulse generator.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfPMA/pma.cfm?id=18437 |title=Premarket Approval (PMA) |access-date=2014-05-05 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506011934/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfPMA/pma.cfm?id=18437 |archive-date=2014-05-06 }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506011934/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfPMA/pma.cfm?id=18437 |date=2014-05-06 }}. FDA "Premarket Approval (PMA) Inspire II Upper Airway Stimulation System" U.S. Food and Drug Administration. April 30, 2014.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Strollo |first1=Patrick J. |last2=Soose |first2=Ryan J. |last3=Maurer |first3=Joachim T. |last4=de Vries |first4=Nico |last5=Cornelius |first5=Jason |last6=Froymovich |first6=Oleg |last7=Hanson |first7=Ronald D. |last8=Padhya |first8=Tapan A. |last9=Steward |first9=David L. |last10=Gillespie |first10=M. Boyd |last11=Woodson |first11=B. Tucker |last12=Van de Heyning |first12=Paul H. |last13=Goetting |first13=Mark G. |last14=Vanderveken |first14=Olivier M. |last15=Feldman |first15=Neil |last16=Knaack |first16=Lennart |last17=Strohl |first17=Kingman P. |title=Upper-Airway Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |date=9 January 2014 |volume=370 |issue=2 |pages=139–149 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa1308659 |pmid=24401051 |s2cid=13764858 }}</ref>

=== Radiofrequency ablation ===
[[Radiofrequency ablation]] (RFA), which is conceptually analogous in some ways to surgery, uses low frequency (300&nbsp;kHz to 1&nbsp;MHz)<ref name="Farrar2008"/> [[radio wave]] energy to target [[tissue (biology)|tissue]], causing [[coagulative necrosis]]. RFA achieves its effects at 40&nbsp;°C to 70&nbsp;°C<ref name="Eick2002"/> unlike other electrosurgical devices which require 400&nbsp;°C to 600&nbsp;°C for efficacy.<ref name="Bashetty2009"/>

Subsequent evaluations of safety and efficacy have led to the recognition of RFA by the [[American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery|American Academy of Otolaryngology]]<ref name="AAO2013"/> as a somnoplasty treatment option in selected situations for mild to moderate OSA, but the evidence was judged insufficient for routine adoption by the American College of Physicians.<ref name=Qa2013/>

RFA has some potential advantages in carefully selected [[medicine|medical]] settings, such as intolerance to the CPAP device. For example, when adherence is defined as greater than four hours of nightly use, 46% to 83% of patients with obstructive sleep apnea are non-adherent with CPAP<ref name="pmid18250209">{{cite journal |last1=Weaver |first1=T. E. |last2=Grunstein |first2=R. R. |title=Adherence to Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Therapy: The Challenge to Effective Treatment |journal=Proceedings of the American Thoracic Society |date=15 February 2008 |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=173–178 |doi=10.1513/pats.200708-119MG |pmid=18250209 |pmc=2645251 }}</ref> for a variety of reasons, including discomfort while sleeping.

RFA is usually performed in an [[outpatient]] setting, using either [[local anesthetic]]s or [[anesthesia awareness|conscious sedation anesthesia]], the procedure itself typically lasting under 3 minutes. The targeted tissue, such as tongue or palate, is usually approached through the mouth without the need for incisions, although occasionally the target is approached through the neck using assisted imaging.<ref name="Steward2005"/> If the tongue is being targeted, this can be done from either [[Anatomical terms of location|dorsal]] or [[ventral]] side. Complications include [[ulceration]], [[infection]], nerve weakness or numbness and swelling. These complications occur in less than 1% of procedures.<ref name="Farrar2008"/>

=== Medications ===
Evidence is insufficient to support the use of medications.<ref name=Qa2013>{{cite journal |last1=Qaseem |first1=Amir |last2=Holty |first2=Jon-Erik C. |last3=Owens |first3=Douglas K. |last4=Dallas |first4=Paul |last5=Starkey |first5=Melissa |last6=Shekelle |first6=Paul |last7=Clinical Guidelines Committee of the American College of |first7=Physicians. |title=Management of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians |journal=Annals of Internal Medicine |date=1 October 2013 |volume=159 |issue=7 |pages=471–483 |doi=10.7326/0003-4819-159-7-201310010-00704 |pmid=24061345 |s2cid=6241714 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gaisl |first1=Thomas |last2=Haile |first2=Sarah R. |last3=Thiel |first3=Sira |last4=Osswald |first4=Martin |last5=Kohler |first5=Malcolm |title=Efficacy of pharmacotherapy for OSA in adults: A systematic review and network meta-analysis |journal=Sleep Medicine Reviews |date=August 2019 |volume=46 |pages=74–86 |doi=10.1016/j.smrv.2019.04.009 |pmid=31075665 |s2cid=149455430 }}</ref><ref name="Gottlieb">{{cite journal |last1=Gottlieb |first1=Daniel J. |last2=Punjabi |first2=Naresh M. |title=Diagnosis and Management of Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Review |journal=JAMA |date=14 April 2020 |volume=323 |issue=14 |pages=1389–1400 |doi=10.1001/jama.2020.3514|pmid=32286648 |s2cid=215759986 }}</ref> This includes the use of [[fluoxetine]], [[paroxetine]], [[acetazolamide]], and [[tryptophan]] among others.<ref name=Qa2013/><ref name=Vea2003>{{cite journal |last1=Veasey |first1=Sigrid C. |title=Serotonin Agonists and Antagonists in Obstructive Sleep Apnea |journal=American Journal of Respiratory Medicine |date=1 February 2003 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=21–29 |doi=10.1007/BF03256636 |pmid=14720019 |s2cid=8288291 }}</ref>

Studies are investigating cannabinoids, especially dronabinol, however, results are not consistent.<ref name="Babson2017">{{cite journal |last1=Babson |first1=Kimberly A. |last2=Sottile |first2=James |last3=Morabito |first3=Danielle |title=Cannabis, Cannabinoids, and Sleep: a Review of the Literature |journal=Current Psychiatry Reports |date=27 March 2017 |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=23 |doi=10.1007/s11920-017-0775-9 |pmid=28349316 |s2cid=7429763 }}</ref> More evidence are needed as many effects of those substances remain unknown, especially the effects of a long-term intake.<ref name="Ramar2018">{{cite journal |last1=Ramar |first1=Kannan |last2=Rosen |first2=Ilene M. |last3=Kirsch |first3=Douglas B. |last4=Chervin |first4=Ronald D. |last5=Carden |first5=Kelly A. |last6=Aurora |first6=R. Nisha |last7=Kristo |first7=David A. |last8=Malhotra |first8=Raman K. |last9=Martin |first9=Jennifer L. |last10=Olson |first10=Eric J. |last11=Rosen |first11=Carol L. |last12=Rowley |first12=James A. |title=Medical Cannabis and the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Position Statement |journal=Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine |date=15 April 2018 |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=679–681 |doi=10.5664/jcsm.7070 |pmid=29609727 |pmc=5886446 }}</ref> The effect on sleepiness and weight gain are particularly of concern.<ref name="Kolla2018">{{cite journal |last1=Kolla |first1=Bhanu Prakash |last2=Mansukhani |first2=Meghna P. |last3=Olson |first3=Eric J. |last4=St. Louis |first4=Erik K. |last5=Silber |first5=Michael H. |last6=Morgenthaler |first6=Timothy I. |title=Medical Cannabis for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Premature and Potentially Harmful |journal=Mayo Clinic Proceedings |date=June 2018 |volume=93 |issue=6 |pages=689–692 |doi=10.1016/j.mayocp.2018.04.011 |pmid=29866280 |s2cid=46936292 }}</ref> Because of uncertainty, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine does not approve the use of medical cannabis for the treatment of OSA.<ref name="Ramar2018" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ramar |first1=Kannan |last2=Kirsch |first2=Douglas B. |last3=Carden |first3=Kelly A. |last4=Rosen |first4=Ilene M. |last5=Malhotra |first5=Raman K. |title=Medical Cannabis, Synthetic Marijuana Extracts, and Obstructive Sleep Apnea |journal=Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine |date=15 October 2018 |volume=14 |issue=10 |pages=1815–1816 |doi=10.5664/jcsm.7412 |pmid=30353829 |pmc=6175803 }}</ref>

==Prognosis==

Stroke and other cardiovascular diseases are related to OSA, and those under the age of 70 have an increased risk of early death.<ref name="Obstructive sleep apnea is a common"/> Persons with sleep apnea have a 30% higher risk of [[heart attack]] or death than those unaffected.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.thoracic.org/sections/publications/press-releases/conference/articles/2007/press-releases/sleep-apnea-increases-risk-of-heart-attack-or-death-by-30.html |title=Sleep Apnea Increases Risk of Heart Attack or Death by 30% | vauthors = Shah NA, Botros NA, Yaggi HK, Mohsenin V |location=New Haven, Connecticut |date=May 20, 2007 |publisher=American Thoracic Society |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090524193435/http://www.thoracic.org/sections/publications/press-releases/conference/articles/2007/press-releases/sleep-apnea-increases-risk-of-heart-attack-or-death-by-30.html |archive-date=May 24, 2009 }}</ref> In severe and prolonged cases, increased in pulmonary pressures are transmitted to the right side of the heart. This can result in a severe form of congestive heart failure known as ''[[cor pulmonale]]''. Diastolic function of the heart also becomes affected.<ref name=pmid24445697>{{cite journal |last1=Sun |first1=Yi |last2=Yuan |first2=Hai |last3=Zhao |first3=Miao-Qing |last4=Wang |first4=Yan |last5=Xia |first5=Ming |last6=Li |first6=Yan-Zhong |title=Cardiac structural and functional changes in old elderly patients with obstructive sleep apnoea–hypopnoea syndrome |journal=Journal of International Medical Research |date=April 2014 |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=395–404 |doi=10.1177/0300060513502890 |pmid=24445697 |s2cid=23011075 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Elevated arterial pressure (i.e., [[hypertension]]) can be a consequence of OSA syndrome.<ref name="Sleep Apnea">{{cite journal | vauthors = Silverberg DS, Iaina A, Oksenberg A | title = Treating obstructive sleep apnea improves essential hypertension and quality of life | journal = American Family Physician | volume = 65 | issue = 2 | pages = 229–236 | date = January 2002 | pmid = 11820487 }}</ref> When hypertension is caused by OSA, it is distinctive in that, unlike most cases (so-called [[essential hypertension]]), the readings do ''not'' drop significantly when the individual is sleeping (non-dipper) or even increase (inverted dipper).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grigg-Damberger |first1=Madeleine |title=Why a Polysomnogram Should Become Part of the Diagnostic Evaluation of Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack |journal=Journal of Clinical Neurophysiology |date=February 2006 |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=21–38 |doi=10.1097/01.wnp.0000201077.44102.80 |pmid=16514349 |s2cid=19626174 }}</ref>

Without treatment, the [[sleep deprivation]] and lack of oxygen caused by sleep apnea increases health risks such as [[cardiovascular disease]], aortic disease (e.g. [[aortic aneurysm]]),<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gaisl T, Bratton DJ, Kohler M | s2cid = 14458813 | title = The impact of obstructive sleep apnoea on the aorta | journal = The European Respiratory Journal | volume = 46 | issue = 2 | pages = 532–544 | date = August 2015 | pmid = 26113685 | doi = 10.1183/09031936.00029315 | doi-access = free }}</ref> [[high blood pressure]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peppard |first1=Paul E. |last2=Young |first2=Terry |last3=Palta |first3=Mari |last4=Skatrud |first4=James |title=Prospective Study of the Association between Sleep-Disordered Breathing and Hypertension |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |date=11 May 2000 |volume=342 |issue=19 |pages=1378–1384 |doi=10.1056/NEJM200005113421901 |pmid=10805822 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lavie |first1=P. |last2=Herer |first2=P |last3=Hoffstein |first3=V |title=Obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome as a risk factor for hypertension: population study |journal=BMJ |date=19 February 2000 |volume=320 |issue=7233 |pages=479–482 |doi=10.1136/bmj.320.7233.479 |pmid=10678860 |pmc=27290 }}</ref> [[stroke]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yaggi |first1=H. Klar |last2=Concato |first2=John |last3=Kernan |first3=Walter N. |last4=Lichtman |first4=Judith H. |last5=Brass |first5=Lawrence M. |last6=Mohsenin |first6=Vahid |title=Obstructive Sleep Apnea as a Risk Factor for Stroke and Death |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |date=10 November 2005 |volume=353 |issue=19 |pages=2034–2041 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa043104 |pmid=16282178 |s2cid=23360654 }}</ref> [[diabetes]], [[clinical depression]],<ref name="pmid15982424">{{cite journal |last1=Schröder |first1=Carmen M |last2=O'Hara |first2=Ruth |title=Depression and Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) |journal=Annals of General Psychiatry |date=2005 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=13 |doi=10.1186/1744-859X-4-13 |pmid=15982424 |pmc=1181621 }}</ref> weight gain, [[obesity]],<ref name = "OSA"/> and even death.

OSA is associated with cognitive impairment, including deficits in inductive and deductive reasoning, attention, vigilance, learning, executive functions, and episodic and working memory. OSA is associated with increased risk for developing [[mild cognitive impairment]] and dementia, and has been associated with neuroanatomical changes (reductions in volumes of the hippocampus, and gray matter volume of the frontal and parietal lobes) which can however be at least in part reversed with CPAP treatment.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gagnon K, Baril AA, Gagnon JF, Fortin M, Décary A, Lafond C, Desautels A, Montplaisir J, Gosselin N | display-authors = 6 | title = Cognitive impairment in obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Pathologie-Biologie | volume = 62 | issue = 5 | pages = 233–240 | date = October 2014 | pmid = 25070768 | doi = 10.1016/j.patbio.2014.05.015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lal C, Strange C, Bachman D | title = Neurocognitive impairment in obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Chest | volume = 141 | issue = 6 | pages = 1601–1610 | date = June 2012 | pmid = 22670023 | doi = 10.1378/chest.11-2214 }}</ref>

==Epidemiology==
OSA (≥ 5 apnea events per hour) in the general population ranges from 9% to 38%, specifically ranging from 13% to 33% in men and 6% to 19% in women, while in the population aged 65 and older, it is as high as 84%, including 90% in men and 78% in women.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | vauthors = Senaratna CV, Perret JL, Lodge CJ, Lowe AJ, Campbell BE, Matheson MC, Hamilton GS, Dharmage SC | display-authors = 6 | title = Prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea in the general population: A systematic review | journal = Sleep Medicine Reviews | volume = 34 | pages = 70–81 | date = August 2017 | pmid = 27568340 | doi = 10.1016/j.smrv.2016.07.002 }}</ref> For ≥&thinsp;15 apnea events per hour, rates ranged from 6% to 17%, and almost 49% prevalence in the older population aged 65 and older.<ref name=":0" /> A 10% increase in body weight led to a 6-fold risk of OSA in obese men and women.<ref name=":0" />

However, OSA is underdiagnosed as it is not always accompanied by daytime sleepiness which can leave the sleep-disordered breathing unnoticed.<ref name="Olaithe_2015">{{cite journal |vauthors=Olaithe M, Nanthakumar S, Eastwood PR, Bucks RS |title=Cognitive and Mood Dysfunction in Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA): Implications for Psychological Research and Practice |journal=Translational Issues in Psychological Science |date=2015 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=67–78 |doi=10.1037/tps0000021 |url=http://research-repository.uwa.edu.au/en/publications/cognitive-and-mood-dysfunction-in-adult-obstructive-sleep-apnoea-osa-implications-for-psychological-research-and-practice(7590bb5c-cb4c-47ae-a09a-62fc73523aea).html |access-date=2023-03-17 |archive-date=2018-05-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180517153656/http://research-repository.uwa.edu.au/en/publications/cognitive-and-mood-dysfunction-in-adult-obstructive-sleep-apnoea-osa-implications-for-psychological-research-and-practice(7590bb5c-cb4c-47ae-a09a-62fc73523aea).html |url-status=live }} {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180517153656/http://research-repository.uwa.edu.au/en/publications/cognitive-and-mood-dysfunction-in-adult-obstructive-sleep-apnoea-osa-implications-for-psychological-research-and-practice(7590bb5c-cb4c-47ae-a09a-62fc73523aea).html |date=2018-05-17 }}</ref> The prevalence of OSA with daytime sleepiness is thus estimated to affect 3% to 7% of men and 2% to 5% of women, and the disease is common in both developed and developing countries.<ref name=punjabi2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Punjabi NM | title = The epidemiology of adult obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Proceedings of the American Thoracic Society | volume = 5 | issue = 2 | pages = 136–43 | date = February 2008 | pmid = 18250205 | pmc = 2645248 | doi = 10.1513/pats.200709-155MG }}</ref> OSA prevalence increases with age and is most commonly diagnosed in individuals over 65 years old, with estimations ranging from 22.1% to 83.6%.<ref name=":0" /> The prevalence has drastically increased in recent decades due to the incidence of obesity.<ref name="Drager2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Drager LF, Togeiro SM, Polotsky VY, Lorenzi-Filho G | title = Obstructive sleep apnea: a cardiometabolic risk in obesity and the metabolic syndrome | journal = Journal of the American College of Cardiology | volume = 62 | issue = 7 | pages = 569–76 | date = August 2013 | pmid = 23770180 | pmc = 4461232 | doi = 10.1016/j.jacc.2013.05.045 }}</ref>

Men are more affected by OSA than women, but the phenomenology differs between both genders.<ref name="OSA" /> Snoring and witnessed apnea are more frequent among men but insomnia for example is more frequent among women.<ref name="OSA" /> The OSA frequency increase with age for the women.<ref name="OSA" /> The mortality is higher for women.<ref name="OSA" />

Some studies report that it is more frequent among the Hispanic and African American population than among the white population.<ref name="OSA" />

If studied carefully in a sleep lab by polysomnography (formal "sleep study"), it is believed that approximately 1 in 5 American adults would have at least mild OSA.<ref name="facial phenotype">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shamsuzzaman AS, Gersh BJ, Somers VK | title = Obstructive sleep apnea: implications for cardiac and vascular disease | journal = JAMA | volume = 290 | issue = 14 | pages = 1906–14 | date = October 2003 | pmid = 14532320 | doi = 10.1001/jama.290.14.1906 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Research==
[[Neurostimulation]] is being studied as a treatment.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kezirian EJ, Boudewyns A, Eisele DW, Schwartz AR, Smith PL, Van de Heyning PH, De Backer WA | title = Electrical stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve in the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea | journal = Sleep Medicine Reviews | volume = 14 | issue = 5 | pages = 299–305 | date = October 2010 | pmid = 20116305 | doi = 10.1016/j.smrv.2009.10.009 }}</ref> An implanted hypoglossal nerve stimulation system received European CE Mark (Conformité Européenne) approval in 2012.<ref>{{cite news |title=ImThera
